entry.title: SAP Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES 15 SP6 – Part 1: Installation, BTP Connection and HTTPS Mapping
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Cloud Connector is the link between SAP BTP and the systems that stay in your own network. This series documents a Linux setup built from scratch in a lab: installation, high availability and an upgrade. Part 1 covers installing Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES 15 SP6, connecting it to a BTP subaccount and exposing an on-premise ABAP system. Part 2 adds a shadow instance, and Part 3 upgrades to 2.19.1. 

Environment

Component Version / detail
Cloud Connector2.16.2
JVMSAP JVM 8.1.112
OSSLES for SAP Applications 15 SP6
Cloud Connector VM4 GB RAM, [vCPU], 32 GB disk, on Proxmox
BackendSAP NetWeaver 7.5 ABAP, MaxDB on a separate host
BTP[trial / productive] subaccount, region [region]

Prerequisites

  • A SLES VM with static IP, working DNS and synchronized time (chronyc tracking), since clock drift breaks the connection to BTP.
  • Outbound HTTPS (443) from the VM to your BTP region, and port 8443 for the Administration UI.
  • The Cloud Connector archive and the SAP JVM RPM from tools.hana.ondemand.com.

Step 1: Install SAP JVM

 

bash
rpm -ivh sapjvm-8.1.112-linux-x64.rpm

The RPM installs to /usr/java/sapjvm_8.1.112 and creates a stable link at /opt/sapjvm_8. I point JAVA_HOME to that link, so a later JVM update does not change the path:

 
bash
cat > /etc/profile.d/sapjvm.sh <<'EOF'
export JAVA_HOME=/opt/sapjvm_8
export PATH=$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH
EOF
source /etc/profile.d/sapjvm.sh
java -version

 

Step 2: Install Cloud Connector

 
bash
mkdir -p sapcc-2.16.2
unzip sapcc-2.16.2-linux-x64.zip -d sapcc-2.16.2
rpm -ivh sapcc-2.16.2/com.sap.scc-ui-*.rpm
systemctl enable --now scc_daemon
systemctl status scc_daemon
ss -tlnp | grep 8443

Step 3: First login

Open https://<host>:8443, log in as Administrator and change the initial password when prompted.

Default Username is Administrator and the Default Password is manage

Step 4: Create a subaccount in the SAP BTP trial

The Cloud Connector always connects to one specific subaccount, so I created a dedicated one for this lab. In the BTP Cockpit of my trial account I chose Create > Subaccount and entered [display name], [region], and [subdomain / default]. [Environment: Cloud Foundry enabled / none]. 

https://cockpit.hanatrial.ondemand.com/trial/

 

 

Once the subaccount was created, I opened its Overview page and noted two values that I need in the next step: the Subaccount ID and the region. 

 

The region matters: the Cloud Connector must be configured with the same region as the subaccount, otherwise it cannot connect.

 

 

 

Step 5: Create the system mapping to the ABAP system

The subaccount is connected, but the Cloud Connector does not expose anything yet. Every backend system has to be released explicitly through a system mapping. A mapping ties an internal host and port, which only exist inside my network, to a virtual host and port, which are the only names BTP ever sees. This keeps the real host names out of the cloud side.

In the Administration UI I opened Cloud To On-Premise, selected the Access Control tab and chose Add to start the wizard.

 

Backend type and protocol. I selected ABAP System as the backend type and HTTP as the protocol. 

 

Internal host and port. I entered the host name of my application server, nw7.sap.local, and the HTTP port of its ICM, 443. The port depends on the instance number. In transaction SMICM, under Goto > Services, you can see which ports the ICM listens on. 

 

Virtual host and port. I chose a generic virtual host, nw7.sap.local, and virtual port, 443. These values are what I will later use in the destination URL, so they should be easy to recognize and should not reveal the real system name. 

Principal type. I selected None, which means no identity is propagated from BTP to the backend. For this first test, authentication is not part of the setup. 

Remaining options. On the summary page I reviewed everything and finished the wizard. 

Exposing a resource. A new mapping exposes nothing by default. I selected the mapping and added a resource under Resources: URL path [/sap/public/ping] with the access policy [Path Only / Path and All Sub-Paths] and the resource set to active. I used this path because it is a lightweight service that needs no logon, and I checked in SICF that the service is active. 

 

Checking availability. Next to the mapping, the Check Availability button returned a green status. This check only confirms that the Cloud Connector can open a TCP connection to the internal host and port. It does not prove that the service answers, and it says nothing about whether BTP can reach it. That test comes in the next step, with a destination in the subaccount. 

Step 6: Create self-signed certificates and establish trust

The Cloud Connector and the ABAP system are separate systems, so each of them has to trust the certificate of the other. For this lab I used self-signed certificates on both sides. In production, certificates from an internal CA are the usual choice.

1. Create a self-signed certificate in the Cloud Connector

In [Configuration > On Premise > System Certificate] I chose [Create and import a self-signed certificate] and entered the host name [scc FQDN] as common name, [key size] and a validity of [period]. [SCREENSHOT: dialog] After saving, the certificate details appeared in the UI. 

 

 

2. Export it

I downloaded the certificate as a .der file , and copied it to the ABAP host:

Step 7: Secure the backend connection with the ABAP SSL server certificate

With a plain HTTP mapping, traffic between the Cloud Connector and the ABAP system is unencrypted. For HTTPS, the Cloud Connector must trust the certificate that the ICM presents. I used a self-signed certificate, which suits a lab. In production, a certificate from an internal CA is the usual choice.

1. Prepare the ABAP system

The ICM needs an HTTPS port, set in the instance profile with icm/server_port_[1] = PROT=HTTPS, PORT=443. In transaction STRUST, under SSL server Standard, I created a self-signed certificate with [nw7 FQDN] as common name. The common name matches the internal host that I use in the mapping. After saving, I restarted the ICM. 

 

2. Export the certificate

I exported the public certificate from STRUST in Base64 format. Only the public certificate leaves the system, never the PSE or a private key. To be sure that this is the certificate the ICM really presents, I compared the fingerprints from the Cloud Connector host:

 

3. Import it into the Backend Trust Store

In the Cloud Connector Administration UI, in [Configuration > On Premise > Backend Trust Store], I chose [Import Certificate] and selected the file. The certificate appeared in the list. 

 

4. Check the mapping

In Cloud To On-Premise > Access Control, in the list Mapping Virtual To Internal System, I [edited the existing mapping / added a new mapping] with protocol HTTPS, internal host [nw7 FQDN] and internal port [HTTPS port]. Then I pressed Check Availability, and the status turned green.

5. Test from BTP

The destination uses an https:// URL with the virtual host and port, Proxy Type OnPremise, and Check Connection succeeded.

 

6. Prove that the trust works

I removed the certificate from the Backend Trust Store and ran the checks again. They failed with [error]. After importing the certificate again, they succeeded. 

Conclusion

You now have a working Cloud Connector 2.16.2 on SLES 15 SP6, running with SAP JVM 8 as a systemd service. It is connected to your SAP BTP subaccount, and it exposes your ABAP system through a system mapping that you verified from BTP with a destination and Check Connection. You also secured the backend connection: by importing the ABAP SSL server certificate into the backend trust store, the Cloud Connector now trusts the system it talks to over HTTPS.

Important Note:

This blog post demonstrates an end-to-end upgrade path and High Availability setup starting from Cloud Connector version 2.16.2 (which is the only legacy version currently available for download on the official SAP Development Tools page).

Please note that version 2.16.2 is no longer supported in production environments. If you are deploying a new Cloud Connector instance from scratch, always download and install the latest available version (2.19.1 or higher) directly.

entry.title: Beat the Single Exclusive Queue Bottleneck : Key-Based JMS Partitioning in SAP Cloud Integration
entry.content:
Beat the Single Exclusive Queue Bottleneck

Key-based JMS partitioning in SAP Cloud Integration — stay in order and process fast

Every integration developer meets this wall sooner or later: "these messages must be processed in order." The easy fix — a single exclusive queue: one consumer, one message at a time — works perfectly and scales terribly. The moment volume rises, that single ordered lane becomes the bottleneck everything queues behind.

Sound familiar? How many times have you "solved" ordering by throttling everything down to one-at-a-time, then watched the backlog grow?

Here's the good news: you almost never need global order. You need order per key. Once you see that, you can keep strict ordering and run in parallel — on plain JMS, no premium add-ons. Let's build the idea up from scratch.

Think of a supermarket, not a single till

Picture a shop with one checkout. Everyone is served in order — beautifully fair, hopelessly slow. The queue out the door isn't a correctness problem; it's a throughput problem.

Now picture several checkout lanes with one rule: the same shopper always goes to the same lane. Each lane still serves its shoppers strictly in order, but different shoppers check out at the same time. Nobody's order is scrambled, and the shop moves.

That's the whole trick. In messaging terms:

  • the lane = a queue processed one message at a time (in order)
  • the shopper = your business key (here, the production order number)
  • "same shopper, same lane" = route each key to a fixed queue

This has a precise name: key-based partitioning with in-order processing — partition by key so each key always lands on the same queue, then process each queue in order with a single consumer. (Database folks will recognise the mechanism as hash sharding: route a hash of the key to one of N stores. Same idea, applied to queues.)

Why "one exclusive queue" hurts

A single ordered queue (in SAP CPI: a JMS queue with Access Type = Exclusive, one consumer, concurrency 1) serializes everything:

One exclusive queue Key-partitioned queues

Order keptGlobally (whole stream)Per key
ParallelismNone — one at a timeUp to N keys at once
ThroughputFloorN× higher
Backlog headroom1 queue's depthN queues' depth

So ask yourself: do order A and order B actually care about each other? Almost never. Only their own messages must stay sequenced. Global ordering is paying for a guarantee the business didn't ask for.

Taking away the ordering you don't need is the whole optimisation.

The pattern, concretely

Give yourself N queues (partitions) and route by a hash of the key:

partition = floorMod( hash(businessKey), N )
queue     = Q_SITE_<partition>

Because the hash depends only on the key, every message for that key lands on the same partition — and because each partition is drained by a single consumer, those messages are processed strictly in order.

Example with N = 2 (real Java hashCode, then mod 2 — even → 0, odd → 1):

Business keypartitionQueue
PO-10010Q_SITE_0
PO-10021Q_SITE_1
PO-10030Q_SITE_0
PO-10041Q_SITE_1
PO-10050Q_SITE_0

And all of one key's messages ride the same lane, in order:

Messages Key Partition Behaviour

PO-1001 msg 1→5PO-1001Q_SITE_0processed 1→2→3→4→5, no overlap
PO-1002 msg 1→5PO-1002Q_SITE_1runs in parallel with PO-1001

Same shopper, same lane — simple, right?

The ceiling to remember: your number of parallel lanes equals the number of JMS queues you allocate. On JMS, partitions aren't free-floating like Kafka — each partition is a real queue, and a tenant has a finite queue budget. So N = how many keys you want in flight at once, capped by available JMS queues (sizing below).

Making it real in SAP Cloud Integration

Want to see how little code this takes? Two iFlows: a dispatcher that routes each message to its partition, and N consumers that each drain one partition in order.

Dispatcher — HTTPS sender → Content Modifier → Groovy → JMS receiver (dynamic queue).

A Content Modifier first promotes the externalized parameters to exchange properties (Groovy can't read {{...}} parameters directly): set partitionLimit = {{partitionLimit}} and site = {{site}}. Then the Groovy derives the partition and sets the target queue name:

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message
import groovy.json.JsonSlurper

Message processData(Message message) {
    // stream the body so the scanner is happy; stream-caching keeps it readable for the JMS send
    def json = new JsonSlurper().parse(message.getBody(java.io.Reader.class))

    def raw = (json.productionOrder ?: '').toString()
    if (!raw?.trim()) throw new IllegalStateException("productionOrder missing — cannot partition")
    def orderNo   = raw.trim().toUpperCase()                 // normalize -> same key, same partition
    def messageNo = (json.messageNo ?: '').toString().trim()

    // partitionLimit (N) is mandatory — fail loudly if the User didn't set the External Parameter
    def limitRaw = message.getProperty('partitionLimit')
    if (limitRaw == null || !limitRaw.toString().trim())
        throw new IllegalStateException("partitionLimit is empty — set it via External Parameter {{partitionLimit}}")
    int n = limitRaw.toString().trim() as int
    if (n < 1) throw new IllegalStateException("partitionLimit must be >= 1 (its set as ${n})")

    def site      = ((message.getProperty('site') ?: 'SITE') as String).trim().toUpperCase()
    int partition = Math.floorMod(orderNo.hashCode(), n)     // deterministic & stable
    def queue     = "Q_${site}_${partition}".toString()      // underscores only; e.g. Q_SITE_0

    message.setProperty('queueName', queue)                  // JMS receiver Queue Name = ${property.queueName}

    def mpl = messageLogFactory?.getMessageLog(message)
    mpl?.addCustomHeaderProperty('orderNo', orderNo)
    mpl?.addCustomHeaderProperty('messageNo', messageNo)
    mpl?.addCustomHeaderProperty('partition', partition.toString())
    mpl?.addCustomHeaderProperty('queueName', queue)
    return message
}

The JMS receiver uses Queue Name = ${property.queueName} (match the capitalisation exactly), Access Type = Exclusive.

Consumer — one per partition (Consumer_SITE_0, Consumer_SITE_1, …). The single setting that creates in-order processing is Number of Concurrent Processes = 1 on the JMS sender adapter.

This consumer iflow is set to throw custom exception/error if the messageNo received in the payload is 3. This is done intentionally to test the exclusivity and negatively test retry case 

How many partitions?

Tempted to spin up one queue per order? Resist it. Two limits get confused:

Limit Meaning Rough size

Transactions per queueHow deep one exclusive queue can get (backlog)150 default, max 500
Number of queuesHow many queues the tenant allows30 default , max 100

A queue is a conveyor belt, not a storage box — thousands of keys flow through a handful of lanes over time. Size N to your peak concurrently-active keys (tens), not your total keys (thousands), within your available JMS queue count.

More lanes than you have concurrent keys is just idle queues. Start small, measure, grow.

See it work

Sample Payload sent from Postman

{
  "productionOrder": "PO-1001",
  "messageNo": "1"
}

Likewise its sent for different productionOrders and the respective related messageNos to it. As per the design until messageNo=3 the partition queue do not get stuck.

Any new messages to this partition gets queued and awaits the stuck message clearance.

However regardless of this stall at Q_SITE_0 other Partitions process messages smoothly



Filter the monitor on a custom header for the key: one key's messages sit on a single queue with non-overlapping timestamps (in order), while a different key runs at the same time on another queue (in parallel). That one screen is the whole argument.

The honest catch: a poison message stalls its lane

Here's the uncomfortable question: when a message simply can't be processed — bad data, a missing lookup — should the line stop, or skip ahead?

On an exclusive partition it stops, by design. The failing message stays at the head of its queue, keeps failing, and the rest of that key's messages wait behind it until someone fixes the data and reprocesses. Crucially, only that one partition stalls — every other key keeps flowing.

Is that a bug? No — it's the guarantee doing its job. Better to halt one order's lane than to halt the only global queue. Just monitor queue depth and keep a reprocessing path ready.

Levelling up

What we hand-built on JMS is exactly what SAP Advanced Event Mesh partitioned queues do natively — set a partition key, and the broker handles ordering, parallel consumers, and rebalancing for you. If AEM is in your entitlement, prefer it. And native parallel Exactly-Once-In-Order is on the Cloud Integration roadmap, which will enable context-based in-order processing, providing fine-grained serialization to avoid bottlenecks due to unrelated messages. Until then, key-based JMS partitioning is the pragmatic path without AEM in landscape.

TL;DR

  • You rarely need global order — only order per key.
  • Partition by key (same key → same JMS queue) and process each queue in order (concurrency 1): ordered and parallel.
  • Parallel lanes = number of JMS queues you allocate; size N to peak concurrent keys, not total volume.
  • Ordering's trade-off: a poison message stalls its own lane — monitor and have a reprocess path.

So — next time someone says "it has to be in order," you've got a better answer than "one at a time." What's the trickiest ordering problem you've had to tame? or Any questions? Tell me in the comments.

Disclosure: I used AI assistance to help draft and structure this post. The design decisions, hands-on build, and testing are my own, and I reviewed and validated the content before publishing.

entry.title: Getting started with Micro-Integrations on Advanced Event Mesh: Access Options & Activation
entry.content:
Not every integration scenario requires a full-fledged integration platform. For some scenarios, all you need is a lightweight way to connect an application or service directly to your event broker.

This is where the Micro-Integrations capability of SAP Integration Suite, advanced Event Mesh comes in.
They provide lightweight integration functionality to easily connect SaaS and legacy applications, LLMs and AI Agents, messaging services, data stores, file servers, etc. directly to your event brokers. It also supports basic transformations, comparable to message mappings.

The keyword here is lightweight. Micro-Integrations are not a replacement for Cloud Integration, it complements it. Cloud Integration is designed to handle integration complexity way beyond the level that the Micro-Integrations capability can handle. Micro-Integrations focus on simplicity, speed, and high volume use cases.

In practice, using Cloud Integration for simple pass-through scenarios from or to Advanced Event Mesh with no transformation (apart from perhaps a message mapping) can be inefficient. In high-volume scenarios (e.g. Event Streaming) it means you’re consuming a lot of messages without leveraging the true strength of Cloud Integration.
This is exactly where the Micro-Integrations capability adds value: handling lightweight, high-throughput integrations, closer to the event broker, while leaving the more complex transformations to Cloud Integration.

The following blog: Small but Great: Introducing Micro-Integrations for Advanced Event Mesh was published when Micro-Integrations were released and provides more background on the capability. I recommend reading it before continuing this blog, as it explains the capability and benefits in more detail, this blog focuses specifically on how to obtain access.

Initially, included with certain broker service classes (as from Broker 1K), now they are also available an an additional chargeable capability. This new metric you can be charged for each hour an additional Micro-Integration is in state "deployed", the pricing can be found on SAP Discovery Center.

The following table shows how many Micro-Integrations (MI) are included with each broker service class, note that each MI can contain up to 5 flows:

Service ClassNr. of Micro-Integrations Included
Broker 100 (Developer)0
Broker 250 (Smallest Production Broker)0
Broker 1K2
Broker 5K5
Broker 10K8
Broker 50K15
Broker 100K25


This new (Micro-Integration by the hour) metric enables organizations to:

  1. Leverage Micro-Integrations when they only have small brokers:
    We recommend having the same broker size for PROD and QA. This means that for a 3 tier environment the smallest setup is Broker 250 for PROD and QA and Broker 100 for DEV. In this case, Micro-Integrations are not included in your broker and if you want to use Micro-Integrations, you need to purchase it as a seperate line item.

  2. Use additional flows:
    Every Micro-Integration comes with 5 flows, a single flow contains the details of a target/source system/queue/topic, error handling config (e.g. Dead Message Queues) and a message mapping.
    So let's say, you have an SFTP source micro-integration, these flows can listen to their own SFTP server or directory/folder and map different objects, for example:
    • 5 flows that listen to the same SFTP server but each to a different directory.
      One listens to the directory /salesorders and maps sales order objects, another one that listens to /businesspartners and maps business partner objects, etc:
      in this case you require 1 Micro-Integration.
    • 5 flows that each listen to a different SFTP server but they both map and publish sales order objects:
      in this case you require 1 Micro-Integration
    • 10 flows that listen to the same SFTP server, but map different objects:
      in this case you require 2 Micro-Integrations
     
  3. Leverage more Micro-Integrations than included in your Broker or Subaccount:
    Micro-Integrations cannot be shared across Subaccounts, so let's say you have a 3 tier environment with a 1K Broker in PROD & QA and a 250 Broker (no MIs included) in DEV, each environment is hosted in a different SAP BTP Subaccount. In this case, you can leverage 2 Micro-Integrations in PROD, 2 in QA (as this is included in your Broker), but if you were to use Micro-Integrations on your DEV Subaccount, you would need to activate the entitlement for additional Micro-Integrations on your DEV Subaccount.
    Following the same example, if you want to use more than 2 Micro-Integrations in your PROD and/or QA environment, you also need to activate the entitlement for additional MIs on your PROD and/or QA Subaccount.


In this blog, we will walk you through the process of enabling the Micro-Integrations add-on within your SAP AEM environment, as well as the activation process of a 1K Broker or larger.

Assigning the entitlements to your SAP BTP Subaccount

In this first part of the blog, we will assign the required entitlements to the SAP BTP Subaccount. Depending on how you want to obtain Micro-Integrations, this can either be the entitlement for the Micro-Integration add-on or an entitlement for a broker service class that includes Micro-Integrations (Broker 1K or larger).
This part of the process needs to be done by the Subaccount or Global Account Administrator on SAP Business Technology Platform.

  1. Go to your SAP BTP Cockpit
  2. Navigate to the SAP BTP Subaccount, where you have deployed an Advanced Event Mesh environment and where you want to enable Micro-Integrations.

     

  3. In your Subaccount, go to "Entitlements", and click on "Edit".

     

  4. Now, click on "Add Service Plan" on the right top of the table.
  5. Look for "integration-suite-advanced-event-mesh". 
  6. Now you should see "SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh", under "Services available to this subaccount", select this service.

     

  7. Under "Available Plans", select "micro-integration-add-on". This entitlement allows you to create additional Micro-Integrations beyond those included with eligible broker service classes.
  8. Optional: If you want to use the Micro-Integratoins included with your broker service, select the appropriate broker entitlement instead. For example, a Broker 1K includes two Micro-Integrations (this is smallest broker that includes MIs) , please have a look at the documentation if you want to know how many Micro-Integrations are included in your broker.
    You can also assign both entitlements if you want to use the Micro-Integrations included with your broker service and additional Micro-Integrations through the add-on.

     

  9. Once you've selected the right service plans, click on "Add Service Plans" at the bottom of your screen.

     

  10. Don't forget to press the "Save" button.

     

     

Optional: Ensure a compatible broker is available

To deploy Micro-Integrations, you need at least one active broker in your Advanced Event Mesh environment. If you are using the Micro-Integrations included with a broker service, the minimum service class is Broker 1K. If you are using the micro-integration-add-on entitlement, any broker service class can be used. This section is written for organizations that want to deploy a broker that already includes Micro-Integration. The following steps are performed by the Mission Control Manager in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh.

  1. In your SAP BTP Subaccount, go to "Instances and Subscription" and open "SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh" (under "Subscriptions").

     

  2. Now, you are redirected to what we refer to as the “Cloud Console” in Advanced Event Mesh (you can always go back to the cloud console by clicking on the SAP logo on the top left).
  3. In the Cloud Console, scroll down to "Mission control" and open "Cluster Manager".

     

  4. In the Cluster Manager you seee an overview of your existing brokers. If you don't have a 1K Broker or a larger broker, click on "Create Service" on the right top.
  5. Provide at least the following:
    • Service Name
    • Cloud provider & region
    • Service Type: Enterprise
    • Service Class: Broker 1K (or larger)
  6. Click on "Create Service". 

     

  7. Once the service is ready, you should see a screen that looks like this (see screenshot below). This means that your broker was successfully created!

Granting access to Micro-Integrations

If you (or your admin) have successfully configured the appropriate Micro-Integration entitlement and/or broker service, we're almost ready to create and deploy Micro-Integrations. The only thing you must verify is that you and/or the people who should create and deploy the MIs, have the "Micro-Integrations Manager" role assigned. This part of the process is done by the Account Administrator in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh.

  1. In the Cloud Console, click on the user icon (bottom left corner) and go to "Account Details".
  2. Now, go to "User Management" ➡️ "Users", click on the 3 dots right next to the user you want to grant access to Micro-Integrations and hit "Edit".

     

  3. Go to the line "Micro-Integrations" and open the drop-down list, select "Micro-Integrations Manager", and press "Save". Now this user will be able to create and deploy Micro-Integrations in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh. Repeat the previous 3 steps to give access to other users.

     

Discovering and creating Micro-Integrations

Once the appropriate entitlement has been assigned, a compatible broker is available, and the Micro-Integrations Manager role has been assigned to your user, you can create and deploy Micro-Integrations.

  1. In the Cloud Console in Advanced Event Mesh, you should now see a tile with the title "Micro-Integrations". Click on this tile.

     

  2. Here, you will find an overview of all Micro-Integrations that are created. Click on "Create Micro-Integration" on the right top.

     

  3. Now, you see an overview of all Micro-Integrations that you can create and configure with Advanced Event Mesh.

     

  4. From this list, you can select a Micro-Integration that fits your use case and start configuring it. Configuring a Micro-Integration is very straight forward, you need the connection and credential details of the source or target system, as well as the queue/topic and broker credentials to create and configure the Micro-Integration.

If you want to try-out a Micro-Integration, I recommend to go through a blog I wrote earlier this year:
File to Mesh: Liberating SFTP Data with Micro-Integrations. 
In this blog, we create a Micro-Integration that listens to an SFTP server and publishes the lines of a CSV file one by one as (mapped) events to the broker. The File to Mesh use case is one where Micro-Integrations are commonly used.

entry.title: Fixing the Orphaned Workflow Issue in SF Time Off Cancellation: withdrawWfRequest using Odata API
entry.content:
The Problem

If you're building a third-party integration either a mobile app, custom portal, or any external system that allows employees to request and cancel time off via SuccessFactors OData APIs, you may have run into this exact issue:

Employee cancels their time off request through your custom app. The EmployeeTime record correctly shows "approvalStatus = CANCELLED" in SF. But the manager still sees the request sitting in their approval inbox now showing a confusing "Cancelled" status that they can't do anything about, because the workflow instance itself was never terminated.

This is a common integration gap, and it happens because the business object and the workflow instance are two separate things in SF, and cancelling one does not automatically close the other.

This post demonstrates the full fix end-to-end, with real request/response payloads.

 

Why This Happens

Object What it represents
What updating it does
EmployeeTime recordThe actual time off data (dates, type, status)Changes the record's own status field only
WfRequest (workflow instance)The routing object sitting in the approver's inboxControls what the manager sees in their To-Do list

The EmployeeTime record and the WfRequest workflow instance are two separate objects in SF. Patching the record's approvalStatus field only changes the record itself it does not notify the workflow engine that the related approval item should close.

As a result, the workflow stays visible on the manager's screen even after the record shows CANCELLED, unless withdrawWfRequest is called explicitly to terminate that workflow instance.

 

The Full Flow: Demonstration

Step 1 - Employee cancels time off (existing working step) from Custom App

Below is the leave request detail Payload which be passed to CPI as request from custom application with Externalcode, User Id (LeaveRequestID), Time Type, Start Date and End Date

{
    "LeaveRequestID": "307eb8b817fd4e6c87f3d6ecdfc88cdf", --> External code of the leave
    "timeType": "1000",
    "userId": "test1",
    "startDate": "2026-10-01T00:00:00.000",
    "endDate": "2026-10-01T00:00:00.000"
}

Post Call: 

At this point, the time record is updated but the workflow is still active on the manager's screen. This is the gap.

Step 2 - Retrieve the associated wfRequestId

Before you can withdraw anything, you need the workflow ID tied to this specific time record. Query it via the navigation property or a filtered lookup:

GET call:

https://<api-server>/odata/v2/EmployeeTime?$select=externalCode,approvalStatus,endDate,startDate,timeType,userId,workflowRequestId&$filter=externalCode eq '${property.externalCode}' --> External code we got from mobile app ( in this case '307eb8b817fd4e6c87f3d6ecdfc88cdf')

Note: The exact navigation property name can differ depending on whether this is a standard object (EmployeeTime) or a custom MDF object . MDF objects typically expose this through a generic workflow association field configured in the object definition. Check your object's metadata ($metadata) if the property name above doesn't match your instance.

Step 3 - Withdraw the workflow (the actual fix)

Use the HTTP Adapter in CPI below screenshot to withdraw the workflow,

 

 

 

 

 


POST Call :
(use the worflow id from step 2) - https://<api-server>/odata/v2/withdrawWfRequest?wfRequestId=1937715L

API Response -

<d:WfRequestActionResponse>
 <d:element m:type="SFOData.WfRequestActionResponse">
<d:status>success</d:status>
<d:wfRequestId m:type="Edm.Int64">1937715L</d:wfRequestId>
 </d:element>
</d:WfRequestActionResponse>

The workflow instance is now terminated. It disappears from the manager's pending approvals, and the workflow history correctly reflects it as Withdrawn rather than leaving a dangling "Cancelled" item with no further action possible.

Pattern

Cancel object → Get wfRequestId → withdrawWfRequest (HTTP Adapter in CPI)

Applies to any standard or custom MDF object with workflow routing.


Error Handling:

 
Error CodeLikely Cause
COE_GENERAL_BAD_REQUESTEither the API user lacks withdrawWfRequest permission in WorkflowAllowedActionList, or the wfRequestId is invalid/already closed
404 on the wfRequestId lookupThe object may not have an active workflow (e.g., auto-approved request with no routing) — handle this gracefully and skip step 3
Permission error on withdrawConfirm this is a separate authorization from the one governing object creation/cancellation — easy to miss since the first two calls can work fine while this one fails

 

Summary

A clean cancellation flow for any workflow-routed object in SuccessFactors requires two actions, not one:

  1. Update the business object's status
  2. Explicitly withdraw the associated workflow instance via withdrawWfRequest

Skipping step 2 is what causes orphaned "Cancelled" items to linger on manager approval screens , a frustrating but entirely avoidable integration bug once you know the workflow engine and the business object are decoupled.

Hope you found this blog helpful, please leave your feedback or any suggestion in the comment. 

Thanks,
Amit

entry.title: SAP API Management–Part 5: Advanced Topics Routing, Developer Hub, Analytics & MCP Gateway
entry.content:
SAP API Management for Beginners – Part 5: Advanced Topics — Routing, Path Removal, Developer Hub, Analytics & MCP Gateway

Part 5 of a 5-part beginner series on SAP API Management within SAP Integration Suite.

A quick recap

Over Parts 1–4, we went from zero to a fully governed API:

Part What we built
1APIM concepts + complete features tour (with real exported XML)
2Northwind_API_V1 proxy — 75 resources, conditional flows, defaultRaiseFaultPolicy
3VerifyAPIKey + Product/Subscription + Debug + Versioning + Policy Templates
4OauthService proxy (APIM-native token generation) + OAuth validation + KVM + Spike Arrest + Quota + JSON Threat Protection + CORS

By the end of Part 4, the Policy/ folder in our exported proxy has 9 XML files, the Proxy Endpoint PreFlow has 5 policy steps, and the Target Endpoint PreFlow has 2 steps (for S/4HANA scenarios).

In this final post, we tackle the patterns that separate beginners from practitioners:

  1. Routing using policies — send requests to different backends dynamically
  2. Path removal and rewriting — clean consumer-facing URLs
  3. Developer Hub — the consumer's self-service perspective
  4. Analytics dashboards — built-in + custom metrics with Statistics Collector
  5. MCP Gateway — expose your APIs as governed MCP servers for AI agents

1. Routing using policies

In a real-world scenario, you often need a single proxy to route requests to different backends based on conditions — URL path, headers, or consumer identity.

1.1 The use case

Say your organization has two environments:

  • Standard consumers → route to the Northwind V2 service
  • Premium consumers → route to a newer V4 service or a dedicated backend

Or: route /customers/* to one backend and /orders/* to another.

1.2 Route Rules in the Proxy Endpoint

Our Northwind_API_V1 proxy has one route rule — all traffic goes to the default Target Endpoint:

 
xml
<routeRules>
    <routeRule>
        <name>default</name>
        <targetEndPointName>default</targetEndPointName>
        <sequence>1</sequence>
    </routeRule>
</routeRules>

You can define multiple Target Endpoints and use Route Rules with conditions to select between them:

 
xml
<routeRules>
    <routeRule>
        <name>premium-route</name>
        <targetEndPointName>PremiumBackend</targetEndPointName>
        <conditions>apiproduct.name = "Premium_Product"</conditions>
        <sequence>1</sequence>
    </routeRule>
    <routeRule>
        <name>default-route</name>
        <targetEndPointName>default</targetEndPointName>
        <sequence>2</sequence>
    </routeRule>
</routeRules>

The first rule that matches wins. Premium consumers (subscribed to Premium_Product) get routed to PremiumBackend. Everyone else falls through to default.

1.3 Dynamic routing with Assign Message

A simpler approach: use an Assign Message policy on the TargetEndpoint PreFlow to dynamically change the target URL at runtime.

Where: TargetEndpoint → PreFlow → Incoming Request

 
xml
<AssignMessage async="false" continueOnError="false" 
               enabled="true" 
               xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <AssignVariable>
        <Name>target.url</Name>
        <Value>https://alternative-backend.example.com/api</Value>
    </AssignVariable>
</AssignMessage>

This overrides the target URL for every request. More useful with a condition — route based on a header, query parameter, or the consumer's product tier.

💡Routing at the gateway level is what makes APIM an integration layer, not just a proxy. Instead of building routing logic in CPI or in the consumer's code, you handle it at the gateway — centralized, visible, and configurable without code changes.

 

2. Path removal and rewriting

This is one of the most common real-world patterns. Your backend has long, complex paths, but you want consumers to call clean, short URLs.

2.1 The problem

Your S/4HANA OData service lives at:

 
https://my12345.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner

You want consumers to call:

 
https://<apim-host>/partners

2.2 Path rewriting with Assign Message

Where: TargetEndpoint → PreFlow → Incoming Request

Step 1: Set your proxy's API Base Path to /partners.

Step 2: Add an Assign Message policy to rewrite the path:

 
xml
<AssignMessage async="false" continueOnError="false" 
               enabled="true" 
               xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Set>
        <Path>/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner</Path>
    </Set>
    <AssignTo createNew="false" type="request"/>
</AssignMessage>

Now when a consumer calls GET /partners?$top=5, APIM translates it to the full S/4HANA path before sending it to the backend.

2.3 Path prefix removal with JavaScript

For more dynamic path manipulation — stripping a prefix, appending a suffix, or transforming the path based on variables — use a JavaScript policy:

Step 1: Add a JavaScript policy to TargetEndpoint PreFlow:

 
xml
<Javascript async="false" continueOnError="false" 
            enabled="true" 
            xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <ResourceURL>jsc://removePathPrefix.js</ResourceURL>
</Javascript>

Step 2: Upload the JavaScript file as a proxy resource (removePathPrefix.js

 
javascript
var originalPath = context.getVariable("proxy.pathsuffix");
// Strip the versioned prefix
var newPath = originalPath.replace("/api/v1", "");
context.setVariable("target.copy.pathsuffix", false);
context.setVariable("target.url", 
    context.getVariable("target.url") + newPath);

💡Path removal is about consumer experience. Your consumers shouldn't need to know your backend's internal URL structure. Give them clean, versioned, RESTful paths — let APIM translate behind the scenes.

⚠️Test path changes with the Debug tool. A missing or extra / in the path rewrite is the most common cause of 404 errors. Debug shows you the outbound request URL — verify it matches what the backend expects.

 

3. Developer Hub — the consumer's perspective

We've been working in the API Portal (admin side). The Developer Hub is what your consumers — partner developers, mobile teams, third-party integrators — actually see.

3.1 What consumers see

Section Content
Home pagePublished Products as cards with descriptions, API counts, and quota info
Product detailAPIs included, quota limits, documentation links
API detailAll resources (from the Resource tab), parameters, example responses
Try Out consoleEmbedded API test tool — send real requests from the browser without Postman
My ApplicationsConsumer's own Applications with API keys and usage stats

 

3.2 The consumer journey

  1. Discover — browse Products, read descriptions, explore API resources
  2. Try Out — test APIs directly in the browser console (no Postman needed)
  3. Subscribe — pick a Product, create an Application, get API key + secret
  4. Build — use the key in their integration
  5. Monitor — check their own usage and remaining quota in the portal

💡The Try Out console is a game changer for developer experience. Instead of emailing API docs, consumers test your APIs live in the browser. The console auto-fills the base URL, handles auth — they pick a resource, add parameters, and hit Send. For our Northwind_API_V1, all 75 resources appear in the console, organized and ready to test.

 

3.3 Self-registration for external consumers

For external developers, enable Self-Registration in Developer Hub settings:

Setting Recommended
Approval required✅Yes (for production) — admin reviews each registration
Email verification✅Yes
Auto-approveOnly for trial/sandbox environments

3.4 Application lifecycle management

From the admin side (API Portal → Manage → Applications

Action When
View all ApplicationsSee who's subscribed and which Products they use
Suspend an ApplicationTemporarily block access — key immediately invalidated, reversible
Revoke an ApplicationPermanently block — consumer needs a new Application and key
View usageSee call counts per Application

⚠️The "unidentified application" pattern: If you see traffic from "Unidentified" in Analytics, it means requests are reaching your proxy without being associated with a registered Application. This could mean VerifyAPIKey is disabled or has continueOnError="true" — check your policy config.

4. Analytics dashboards

4.1 Built-in analytics

Go to Analyze APIs from the Integration Suite launchpad. Three views:

Overview (Executive view):

KPI What it shows
Total TrafficTotal API calls for the selected period
Average Response TimeMean latency in ms
Total Errors4xx + 5xx count
Top APIs by TrafficMost-called proxies
Top ApplicationsMost active consumers
Slowest APIsProxies with highest latency
Response Code Distribution2xx vs 4xx vs 5xx ratios

 

Health (DevOps view):

Error trends (4xx vs 5xx over time), response time percentiles (P50, P90, P95), error breakdown by proxy and response code.

💡The 401 vs 429 vs 500 breakdown is your diagnostic starting point:

  • High 401 → consumers misconfiguring API keys or OAuth tokens (education problem)
  • High 429 → consumers hitting Spike Arrest or Quota limits (capacity problem)
  • High 500 → backend failing or policy misconfiguration like unresolved KVM variables (infrastructure problem)

Usage (Product Manager view):

Traffic by Product, Application, and Developer. API call distribution across resources.

4.2 Custom dashboards with Statistics Collector

Need to track something specific — like which Northwind Customers are queried most?

Step 1: Add an Extract Variables policy (ProxyEndpoint PostFlow, Outgoing Response):

 
xml
<ExtractVariables async="true" continueOnError="true" 
                   enabled="true" 
                   xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <URIPath>
        <Pattern ignoreCase="true">/Customers('{customerId}')</Pattern>
    </URIPath>
    <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>true</IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>
</ExtractVariables>

⚠️Note continueOnError="true" here. Not every request will match the pattern (list requests don't have a CustomerID in the path). We don't want the policy to fail on non-matching URLs.

Step 2: Add a Statistics Collector policy right after:

 
xml
<StatisticsCollector async="false" continueOnError="false" 
                      enabled="true" 
                      xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Statistics>
        <Statistic name="customerId" ref="customerId" type="string">unknown</Statistic>
    </Statistics>
</StatisticsCollector>

The unknown default is used when the variable isn't resolved (e.g., on a list request).

Step 3: Go to Analyze → dropdown → Custom View → create a chart with customerId as the dimension.

💡This is powerful for business intelligence. Your product owner can see: "Customer ALFKI is queried 500 times a day by the 3PL integration, but BERGS is only queried twice." That's actionable — maybe the 3PL should be caching ALFKI's data.

5. MCP Gateway — expose APIs for AI agents

This is the newest capability in SAP Integration Suite — and the one that positions your APIs for the agentic era.

5.1 What is MCP?

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the open standard that lets AI agents discover and call tools at runtime — without hardcoded integrations.

 
Without MCP:  Developer hardcodes API endpoints into agent tool definitions
With MCP:     Agent connects to MCP server → discovers tools from metadata → calls them

Think of MCP as "USB-C for AI agents" — a universal plug that lets any agent connect to any tool server.

5.2 How MCP Gateway works in Integration Suite

The MCP Gateway sits on top of the API proxies we've already built:

 
AI Agent (Claude Desktop / Copilot Studio / Cline / Joule)
    ↓ Streamable HTTP + OAuth Bearer token
MCP Gateway (SAP Integration Suite)
    ↓ All existing policies apply (APIKey, Quota, Spike Arrest, etc.)
API Artifact (Northwind_API_V1 or any managed API)
    ↓
Backend (Northwind / S/4HANA / any system)

All your existing policies still apply — the agent is just another consumer, accessing through MCP instead of direct HTTP. The MCP endpoint follows a standard pattern:

 
https://<your-apim-host>/mcp/v1/<server-name>

5.3 Prerequisites

Prerequisite Details
Integration Suite editionPremium, Enhanced, or Trial (Free Plan)
Capabilities activatedCloud Integration AND API Management
Integration Cell runtimeEnabled and Active (Settings → Runtimes)
RolePI_Integration_Developer assigned to your user

⚠️MCP Servers run on Integration Cell, not the classic Cloud Integration runtime. Go to Settings → Runtimes and confirm Integration Cell shows as Active.

5.4 Three source types for MCP Servers

SAP Integration Suite supports three ways to create an MCP Server:

Source type What it does Best for
APICreate from an existing API artifact deployed on Integration CellOur Northwind proxy — most common
HTTP Endpoint + OpenAPI specImport an OpenAPI specification and expose operations from any HTTP endpointThird-party REST APIs without an APIM proxy
RFCExpose SAP RFC-enabled function modules as MCP toolsDirect S/4HANA or ECC RFC access

We'll use the API approach — creating the MCP Server from our Northwind_API_V1 proxy.

5.5 Create the MCP Server

Step 1: In Integration Suite, navigate to Design → select an Integration Package (or create one).

Step 2: Click Add → MCP Server.

Step 3: Select the source:

Field Value
Source TypeAPI
API ArtifactNorthwind_API_V1

Step 4: Configure the MCP Server details:

Field Value Notes
NameNorthwind_MCPInternal identifier
MCP Path/northwind-toolsUnique path — the full URL becomes https://<host>/mcp/v1/northwind-tools
DescriptionTools to search and retrieve Customers, Orders, and Products from the Northwind demo service. Supports OData filtering, pagination, and entity relationships.Write this for the AI agent — it uses this to decide relevance

⚠️The MCP Path must be unique across all MCP Servers in your tenant. Choose a descriptive, hyphenated name.

5.6 Select and describe tools

The MCP Server auto-discovers resources from your API artifact and presents them as potential tools. You select which ones to expose.

Step 1: Review the discovered resources. For our 75-resource Northwind proxy, you'll see all entity sets, navigation properties, and views.

Step 2: Select the tools to expose. For a beginner setup, start with the core operations:

Tool to expose Source resource Why
GET /CustomersCustomers (collection)List/search customers
GET /Customers('{CustomerID}')Customers (by key)Get a specific customer
GET /Customers('{CustomerID}')/OrdersCustomer's Orders (navigation)Orders for a customer
GET /ProductsProducts (collection)List/search products
GET /OrdersOrders (collection)List/search orders
GET /Orders({OrderID})/Order_DetailsOrder Details (navigation)Line items for an order

Step 3: For each selected tool, write a clear description:

Tool Auto-generated description Your enhanced description
GET /Customers"Retrieves Customers entities""Search for customers by company name, country, or city. Returns CustomerID, CompanyName, ContactName, Address, City, Country. Use OData $filter for specific criteria, e.g., $filter=Country eq 'Germany'"
GET /Products"Retrieves Products entities""List products with name, price, stock level, and category. Filter by price range with $filter=UnitPrice gt 20. Use $top and $skip for pagination"

💡Tool descriptions are the most important part of an MCP Server. The AI agent reads these descriptions to decide which tool to call and how to construct parameters. A vague description means the agent either picks the wrong tool or sends wrong parameters. Write them as if you're explaining the API to a smart colleague who's never seen Northwind.

 

5.7 Deploy and publish

Step 1: Click Deploy. The MCP Server deploys to the Integration Cell runtime.

Step 2: After successful deployment, the MCP Server is available at:

 
https://<your-apim-host>/mcp/v1/northwind-tools

Step 3: Publish to Developer Hub — this makes the MCP Server discoverable alongside your traditional API Products.

 

5.8 Connect Claude Desktop

Configure Claude Desktop to connect to your MCP Server:

 
json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "northwind-tools": {
      "type": "url",
      "url": "https://<your-apim-host>/mcp/v1/northwind-tools",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer <oauth-access-token>"
      }
    }
  }
}

The OAuth token comes from the OauthService proxy we built in Part 4 — or from SAP BTP's OAuth endpoint if you're using platform-level auth.

Once connected, test with a natural language query:

User: "Find all customers in Germany"

Claude: calls GET /Customers with $filter=Country eq 'Germany'

"I found 11 customers in Germany. Here are the first few: Alfreds Futterkiste (Berlin), Blauer See Delikatessen (Mannheim)..."

5.9 Connect other MCP clients

The MCP Gateway uses Streamable HTTP as the transport protocol. Any MCP-compatible client works:

Client Configuration
Claude DesktopmcpServers in settings JSON (shown above)
Cline (VS Code)MCP server configuration in Cline settings
Microsoft Copilot StudioMCP Server connection with OAuth 2.0 via Entra ID trust
SAP JouleNative integration — Joule agents can consume MCP servers from Integration Suite directly
Custom agentsAny MCP client library — connect over Streamable HTTP with OAuth Bearer token

5.10 Governance considerations for AI agents

Exposing APIs to AI agents introduces new patterns:

Rate limiting for agents:

AI agents burst faster than humans — "compare customers in Germany vs France" fires two API calls in milliseconds. Consider:

Approach Configuration
Agent-specific ProductCreate a separate Product with higher Spike Arrest limits for MCP Applications
Burst-aware quotaUse type="flexi" instead of type="calendar" for sliding-window quota

Start with read-only access:

For safety, only expose GET operations as MCP tools initially. Enable write operations (POST, PUT, DELETE) only after validating the agent's behavior in a test environment.

⚠️An agent that can read "Get Customers" is useful. An agent that can write "Delete Customer" is powerful — and risky. Start read-only, validate, then gradually expand.

PII protection:

AI agents may send API responses to external LLMs for processing. Consider adding Assign Message policies that strip sensitive fields (bank details, tax IDs) from responses when the request comes from an MCP-registered Application.

SAP's architectural guidance:

Pattern Protocol Use case
Tool consumptionMCPAgent calls your APIs as tools
Agent delegationA2A (Agent-to-Agent)One agent delegates a task to another

MCP Gateway handles the first pattern. SAP's Agent Gateway (for Joule agents) handles the second. Both are complementary.

6. The complete series — what we've built

Layer Component Part
ConceptsAPIM features tour, architecture, real exported XML1
API ProviderNorthwind_API (+ S/4HANA guidance)2
API ProxyNorthwind_API_V1 — 75 resources, conditional flows, versioned2
Method governanceAuto-generated conditional flows + defaultRaiseFaultPolicy (405)2
SecurityVerifyAPIKey + OauthService (APIM-native token generation) + ValidateOAuthToken3, 4
TrafficSpike Arrest + Quota (with dynamic Product limits)4
Payload securityJSON Threat Protection4
Browser accessCORS headers via Assign Message4
Backend authKVM + Basic Authentication (for S/4HANA scenarios)4
GovernanceProducts, Subscriptions, Policy Templates, Versioning3
Advanced routingRoute Rules, Assign Message path rewriting, JavaScript5
Consumer portalDeveloper Hub, self-registration, Try Out console5
AnalyticsBuilt-in dashboards + custom metrics via Statistics Collector5
AI agentsMCP Gateway — MCP Server from API artifact, Streamable HTTP5

Every layer builds on the previous one. The MCP Gateway reuses the same policies — the agent is just another consumer. The Analytics dashboards show MCP traffic alongside traditional API traffic. That's the compounding value of getting the foundation right.

7. Key lessons from this series

Looking back, there are a handful of insights that prevent 80% of beginner mistakes:

ProxyEndpoint vs TargetEndpoint. Consumer-facing policies (auth, throttling, CORS) go on the Proxy Endpoint. Backend-facing policies (KVM, credential injection) go on the Target Endpoint. This is the APIM equivalent of the Event Mesh credential direction insight (Event Mesh key vs CPI runtime key). Once it clicks, everything falls into place.

XML element ordering. APIM enforces strict element order in policy XML. Source before limits in JSONThreatProtection. Allow → Interval → Distributed → StartTime → Synchronous → TimeUnit in Quota. The error messages point to the element that's out of place, not the one that should be there — check the policy template for the correct sequence.

Case sensitivity. The APIKey header is case-sensitive. APIKey ≠ apikey ≠ Apikey. Same gotcha as Event Mesh queue names (3PL vs 3pl).

OAuth body vs headers. client_id and client_secret go in the request body as x-www-form-urlencoded — not in headers. Same as the XSUAA token endpoint in Event Mesh.

Save ≠ Deploy ≠ Version. Save creates a revision (undo). Deploy makes it live. A Version is a separate proxy (V1 → V2). Revisions for iterating, versions for breaking changes.

Conditional flows are free governance. When you create a proxy from an OData service using Discover, APIM auto-generates conditional flows for every resource with HTTP method enforcement. 75 resources × correct method restrictions, generated in one click. Most tutorials make you do this manually.

Quick Reference

Item How
RoutingTarget Endpoint → Route Rules with conditions, or Assign Message to set target.url
Path removalTarget EP PreFlow → Assign Message with <Set><Path>...</Path></Set>
JavaScript policyUpload .js file as proxy resource, reference via <ResourceURL>jsc://filename.js</ResourceURL>
Developer HubIntegration Suite launchpad → Developer Hub tile
Self-RegistrationDeveloper Hub → Settings → Enable
AnalyticsAnalyze APIs → Overview / Health / Usage
Custom DashboardAnalyze → Custom View → Create with Statistics Collector dimensions
MCP Gateway prereqsIntegration Cell Active + Premium/Enhanced/Trial edition + PI_Integration_Developer role
MCP Source typesAPI artifact, HTTP Endpoint + OpenAPI spec, or RFC
MCP Endpointhttps://<host>/mcp/v1/<server-name>
Claude DesktopmcpServers config with type: "url" + gateway URL + OAuth Bearer token

Wrapping up the series

When we started in Part 1, the question was simple: why can't you just give consumers the direct API URL? Five posts later, the answer spans security, traffic management, OAuth token generation, consumer experience, analytics, and AI-agent readiness.

SAP API Management gives you a single governed layer that stacks cleanly:

  • API Provider → connects to the backend once
  • API Proxy → wraps it with policies and conditional flows
  • OauthService → generates tokens without any external IdP
  • Product → packages proxies for different consumer tiers
  • Developer Hub → lets consumers self-serve
  • Analytics → shows you what's happening
  • MCP Gateway → extends everything to AI agents

Everything reuses what came before. The MCP Gateway doesn't need new policies — it uses the same ones. The Analytics dashboards show MCP data alongside traditional API data. The OauthService proxy issues tokens for both human consumers and AI agents.

And every real error we hit during testing — XML element ordering, OAuth body vs headers, KVM variable resolution, case sensitivity — is now documented in the troubleshooting tables. That's the value of building hands-on instead of just reading documentation.

Thank you for following along. If you've built something with this series, I'd love to hear about it in the comments.

entry.title: Terraform + SAP BTP Trial: Build an Integration Suite Lab from Scratch
entry.content:
Terraform + SAP BTP Trial: Build an Integration Suite from Scratch

 

Figure 1 — Original conceptual illustration created for this tutorial (not a product screenshot).

Have you ever created the same SAP BTP subaccount, assigned entitlements, subscribed to applications, and configured destinations again and again? Terraform helps us describe the desired platform setup in text files and reproduce it consistently.

In this beginner-friendly tutorial, we will create a new BTP subaccount, allocate the Integration Suite trial entitlement, subscribe to Integration Suite, grant initial and developer access, and create a dummy HTTP destination. We will also activate the Cloud Integration capability in the browser—a deliberate manual step that Terraform does not currently cover through this BTP provider.

Important for trial users: An SAP BTP trial may allow only one Integration Suite tenant per global trial account. SAP also preassigns trial entitlements to the default subaccount, so you may need to move the entitlement before a second subaccount can use it. Do not unsubscribe or remove an existing Integration Suite tenant just to follow this blog unless you deliberately want to replace it.

This is not for production usage.

What we will create

 

Figure 2 — Original learning architecture. The workstation is local; subaccount, entitlements, access and destination live in SAP BTP.

Component

What it means

Who creates it?

BTP subaccount

Our new isolated learning area

Terraform

Integration Suite entitlement

Permission to use the trial service plan

Terraform, if trial quota is available

Integration Suite subscription

Tenant/app subscription

Terraform, if the application can be subscribed in this account

Integration_Provisioner

Lets our user access and manage Integration Suite capabilities

Terraform

Cloud Integration capability

Enables the integration tooling

Manual: Integration Suite web UI

PI_Integration_Developer

Lets our user develop integration artifacts

Terraform, after capability activation

HTTP_DEMO destination

Example connection pointing to a public endpoint

Terraform

 

A useful mental model: Entitlement = permission to use a service. Subscription = actually subscribing to its application. Capability activation = enabling a particular function. Role collection = granting a user access. None of these is interchangeable.

1. Prerequisites: install everything locally

We assume Windows 11, a BTP trial global account, and the right to create subaccounts and assign entitlements. All commands in this section run in your local Windows PowerShell terminal, not inside the BTP cockpit.

Install Visual Studio Code, Terraform and SAP BTP CLI

Open PowerShell (Start > type PowerShell) and run:

winget install --id Microsoft.VisualStudioCode -e
winget install --id Hashicorp.Terraform -e
winget install SAP.btp --source winget

 

If Windows reports that one application is already installed, that is fine. Restart PowerShell or VS Code after installing, so the executables appear on your PATH. If winget is unavailable, install VS Code, Terraform, and the SAP BTP CLI from their official download pages.

Verify:

code --version
terraform -version
btp --version

 

In VS Code, select Extensions (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for HashiCorp Terraform, and install the official extension. Or run code --install-extension HashiCorp.terraform from PowerShell.

Why three tools? VS Code is the editor. Terraform is the infrastructure-as-code engine. SAP BTP CLI is our login helper (and optionally useful for checking resources). Terraform itself installs the SAP/btp provider automatically when we run terraform init.

Sign in once, using browser-based SSO

The SAP BTP Terraform provider v1.26.0 can reuse an active btp CLI session. This avoids storing the password in a .tf file. In PowerShell:

btp login --sso
$Env:USE_BTPCLI_SESSION = "true"

 

A browser login will open. Select your trial global account when prompted. Check btp --help if unsure of your installed CLI command options. Keep this terminal open while running Terraform.

No API keys or passwords should go into the public sample code, `terraform.tfvars`, Git, or screenshots.

2. Identify your global account and region in the BTP cockpit

Open the SAP BTP trial cockpit and enter the trial global account. Note the global account subdomain (often ending in trial-ga). This is the value expected by provider "btp"—not the UUID/GUID. Choose a region that your trial global account actually makes available. The example uses us10 because it is common in SAP tutorials, but the correct region is determined by your account.

 

Figure 3 — Anonymized version of a real BTP cockpit screenshot supplied for this exercise. The new Terraform lab should be a new subaccount, not a rename of the existing one.

Trial entitlement warning: The default trial subaccount may already hold the available Integration Suite service plan, even if it is not subscribed. Check Global Account > Entitlements > Entity Assignments, or the equivalent navigation in your cockpit. If it is assigned exclusively to another subaccount, move it to this lab if doing so is safe. The steps and navigation can change between cockpit releases.

3. Open a real project in VS Code

Run the following in the local PowerShell terminal:

mkdir C:\btp-terraform-suite
cd C:\btp-terraform-suite
code .

 

Create these project files in the VS Code Explorer.

C:\btp-terraform-suite\
  providers.tf
  variables.tf
  terraform.tfvars
  01-subaccount.tf
  outputs.tf
  .gitignore

 

What goes in each file?

The following is the complete source, not pseudocode. Our first run creates only the subaccount and reads entitlement information. We add other resources in stages, so it is easy to diagnose mistakes.

`providers.tf`

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"

  required_providers {
    btp = {
      source  = "SAP/btp"
      version = "~> 1.26.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "btp" {
  # Subdomain, NOT the global account GUID.
  globalaccount = var.globalaccount_subdomain
  # Authentication comes from an active btp CLI SSO session.
}

 

`variables.tf`

variable "globalaccount_subdomain" {
  description = "Your BTP global account subdomain (not the GUID)"
  type        = string
}

variable "subaccount_name" {
  description = "Visible name in BTP cockpit"
  type        = string
  default     = "TF Integration Lab"
}

variable "subaccount_subdomain" {
  description = "Unique subdomain for the lab; change this!"
  type        = string
}

variable "region" {
  description = "Choose an available trial region. us10 is an example."
  type        = string
  default     = "us10"
}

variable "developer_username" {
  description = "Exact username in BTP Security > Users"
  type        = string
}

variable "integration_entitlement_service_name" {
  description = "Get this EXACT value from the entitlement_catalog output"
  type        = string
  default     = "integrationsuite-trial"
}

variable "integration_app_name" {
  description = "Get this EXACT value from subscription_candidates output"
  type        = string
  default     = "integration-suite-trial"
}

 

`terraform.tfvars.example`

# COPY this file to terraform.tfvars, then replace ALL examples.
globalaccount_subdomain = "CHANGE-ME-trial-ga"
subaccount_name         = "TF Integration Lab"
subaccount_subdomain    = "tf-suite-lab-youruniqueid"
region                  = "us10"
developer_username      = "your-user@example.com"

# Check outputs before keeping these examples!
integration_entitlement_service_name = "integrationsuite-trial"
integration_app_name                 = "integration-suite-trial"

 

`01-subaccount.tf`

# Step 1: Create one BTP subaccount.
resource "btp_subaccount" "lab" {
  name      = var.subaccount_name
  subdomain = var.subaccount_subdomain
  region    = var.region
  description = "Terraform learning lab for SAP Integration Suite"
}

 

`outputs.tf`

# Discover the exact entitlement service and plan names.
data "btp_globalaccount_entitlements" "catalog" {}

output "entitlement_catalog" {
  description = "Look up the Integration Suite trial plan before Step 2"
  value = [
    for item in values(data.btp_globalaccount_entitlements.catalog.values) : {
      service_display_name = item.service_display_name
      service_name         = item.service_name
      plan_name            = item.plan_name
      quota_remaining      = item.quota_remaining
    }
    if strcontains(lower(item.service_display_name), "integration suite")
  ]
}

output "lab_subaccount_id" {
  value = btp_subaccount.lab.id
}

output "lab_subaccount_name" {
  value = btp_subaccount.lab.name
}

 

4. Run Terraform for the first time

In VS Code > Terminal > New Terminal, choose PowerShell. Verify the path shows C:\btp-terraform-suite. If you opened a new terminal after logging in, set the BTP session flag again:

$Env:USE_BTPCLI_SESSION = "true"
terraform init
terraform fmt
terraform validate
terraform plan
terraform apply

 

When Terraform asks `Enter a value: yes`, type yes and press Enter. Do not use -auto-approve during your first learning exercises.

What should you see? Terraform proposes one btp_subaccount.lab resource, followed by a confirmation that resources were added. In the BTP cockpit's subaccount list, you should see TF Integration Lab (or your chosen name). Use terraform state list to confirm the managed resource. It is normal for output-only data sources to appear in state as well.

The output entitlement_catalog is our safety check. It reports the service's technical service_name, plan_name, and remaining quota. Do not guess these strings from the display name.

terraform output entitlement_catalog
terraform output lab_subaccount_id

 

If entitlement_catalog is empty, the Integration Suite trial plan may not be available to this global account or region. Stop and check entitlements before the next step.

5. Add the Integration Suite trial entitlement

An entitlement says that this subaccount is permitted to consume a service plan. It does not subscribe to Integration Suite.

The example default integrationsuite-trial is an illustrative technical service identifier used in trial-related configurations; use the exact `service_name` in your `entitlement_catalog` output, even if it differs. In terraform.tfvars, update integration_entitlement_service_name accordingly.

From the ZIP's terraform/steps folder, copy `02-entitlement.tf` to your open project folder and run the commands below. Here is the full file:

`02-entitlement.tf`

# Step 2: Add the Integration Suite application entitlement.
# IMPORTANT: Confirm the service_name and plan_name with the
# `entitlement_catalog` output BEFORE terraform apply.
resource "btp_subaccount_entitlement" "integration_suite" {
  subaccount_id = btp_subaccount.lab.id
  service_name  = var.integration_entitlement_service_name
  plan_name     = "trial"
}

 

terraform fmt
terraform plan
terraform apply

 

Check BTP Cockpit > Your new subaccount > Entitlements. You should find an Integration Suite trial application/service plan, provided quota was available.

Failure tip: If SAP BTP reports that the quota is exhausted or the service plan cannot be assigned, Terraform cannot create additional trial entitlements out of nothing. Inspect assignments to other subaccounts and move only unused quota you are authorized to move.

6. Discover the subscription name, then subscribe

Here is a common trap: The entitlement service name and the application subscription name are not guaranteed to be identical. Do not set the subscription app_name to a guessed value merely because the Cockpit displays “Integration Suite.”

Copy `03a-discover-subscription.tf` into your project and run terraform plan, then terraform apply to record the output if required. The data source lists the multitenant applications the subaccount may subscribe to.

`03a-discover-subscription.tf`

# Step 3A: Find the app_name to subscribe to, AFTER entitlement.
data "btp_subaccount_subscriptions" "available" {
  subaccount_id = btp_subaccount.lab.id
  depends_on = [btp_subaccount_entitlement.integration_suite]
}

output "subscription_candidates" {
  value = [
    for app in data.btp_subaccount_subscriptions.available.values : {
      display_name = app.display_name
      app_name     = app.app_name
      plan_name    = app.plan_name
      state        = app.state
    }
    if strcontains(lower(app.display_name), "integration suite")
  ]
}

 

terraform plan
terraform apply
terraform output subscription_candidates

 

Read the item whose display_name is Integration Suite and whose plan_name is trial. Use its `app_name` as integration_app_name in terraform.tfvars. The sample uses integration-suite-trial as a starting example, but the correct value is what your provider reports.

Now copy `03b-subscription.tf` into your project:

`03b-subscription.tf`

# Step 3B: Subscribe to Integration Suite.
# Check integration_app_name against subscription_candidates first.
resource "btp_subaccount_subscription" "integration_suite" {
  subaccount_id = btp_subaccount.lab.id
  app_name      = var.integration_app_name
  plan_name     = "trial"

  depends_on = [btp_subaccount_entitlement.integration_suite]
  timeouts = {
    create = "30m"
  }
}

 

terraform fmt
terraform plan
terraform apply

 

This can take several minutes. Verify in BTP Cockpit > Services > Instances and Subscriptions that Integration Suite shows as subscribed.

Stop if the application is already subscribed elsewhere: Official SAP guidance states that trial accounts may have only one Integration Suite tenant. Moving entitlements or repeating terraform apply will not create another tenant beyond that limit. For a previously existing subscription, importing it into Terraform state requires a separate, deliberate state-management exercise.

7. First access role: Integration_Provisioner

Before you can open Integration Suite and activate features, assign yourself the initial `Integration_Provisioner` role collection. The value developer_username should match the actual identity found under BTP Cockpit > Security > Users; it is not always identical to the email used at login, particularly with custom identity providers.

Copy `04-provisioner.tf` into the project:

`04-provisioner.tf`

# Step 4: Give yourself initial access to manage suite capabilities.
resource "btp_subaccount_role_collection_assignment" "provisioner" {
  subaccount_id      = btp_subaccount.lab.id
  role_collection_name = "Integration_Provisioner"
  user_name          = var.developer_username

  depends_on = [btp_subaccount_subscription.integration_suite]
}

 

terraform plan
terraform apply

 

If the role collection is not yet visible, wait for subscription provisioning to finish, verify it exists in Security > Role Collections, and retry. Sign out and back in when testing newly assigned roles.

8. The required browser step: activate Cloud Integration

This step happens in your web browser—not VS Code. In the BTP cockpit, open Instances and Subscriptions > Integration Suite > Go to Application. Once the Integration Suite landing page loads, select Add Capabilities / Activate Capabilities (wording depends on the UI). Choose the capability that enables Cloud Integration—often labeled Design, Develop, and Operate Integration Scenarios—and finish the activation wizard. Wait for the capability to become active.

SAP's BTP provider handles application subscription, but this is not the same as managing Integration Suite's in-app capability provisioning. Do not claim Terraform has completed Cloud Integration activation merely because the subscription resource applied successfully.

9. Give your user the real Cloud Integration developer role

You requested an Integration_Developer role. For the Cloud Integration capability, the standard role collection identified in SAP's setup documentation is actually `PI_Integration_Developer`. These names matter: Terraform asks SAP BTP for an exact role collection name.

After the Cloud Integration capability is active, copy `05-developer.tf` into the project:

`05-developer.tf`

# Step 5: Add AFTER activating Cloud Integration in the browser.
# The actual Cloud Integration role collection is PI_Integration_Developer.
resource "btp_subaccount_role_collection_assignment" "developer" {
  subaccount_id        = btp_subaccount.lab.id
  role_collection_name = "PI_Integration_Developer"
  user_name            = var.developer_username

  depends_on = [btp_subaccount_subscription.integration_suite]
}

 

terraform plan
terraform apply

 

Verify under BTP Cockpit > Security > Users > your user > Role Collections. You should see Integration_Provisioner and PI_Integration_Developer. Log out and in again if navigation is missing. Administrators may need additional role collections such as PI_Administrator, but we deliberately avoid unnecessary elevated permissions in this learner exercise.

10. Create a dummy HTTP destination with Terraform

Finally, let’s provision something we can see immediately under Connectivity > Destinations. A destination is a named connectivity configuration. Here we define `HTTP_DEMO`, targeting https://httpbin.org/get over the Internet, using NoAuthentication. It contains no passwords or secrets.

The current provider recommends `btp_subaccount_destination_generic` for new examples instead of the older specialized HTTP destination resource. Copy `06-destination.tf`:

`06-destination.tf`

# Step 6: A dummy subaccount-level HTTP destination.
# This is a public endpoint. No credentials are needed.
resource "btp_subaccount_destination_generic" "demo" {
  subaccount_id = btp_subaccount.lab.id

  destination_configuration = jsonencode({
    Name           = "HTTP_DEMO"
    Type           = "HTTP"
    URL            = "https://httpbin.org/get"
    ProxyType      = "Internet"
    Authentication = "NoAuthentication"
    Description    = "Terraform demo destination - safe to delete"
  })
}

 

terraform fmt
terraform validate
terraform plan
terraform apply
terraform state list

 

Now navigate to BTP Cockpit > Your subaccount > Connectivity > Destinations, locate HTTP_DEMO, and optionally choose Check Connection. A saved destination and a successful network test are different things; the test depends on the target endpoint and available connectivity. If creation returns HTTP 403, confirm that your user/identity has subaccount or Destination Administrator permissions and that the destination APIs are available to your trial subaccount.

11. How to confirm everything worked

Where to look

Expected result

Cockpit > Subaccounts

New TF Integration Lab subaccount

Subaccount > Entitlements

Integration Suite trial plan

Subaccount > Instances and Subscriptions

Integration Suite subscribed

Integration Suite home

Cloud Integration capability active

Security > Users > your user

Integration_Provisioner, PI_Integration_Developer

Connectivity > Destinations

HTTP_DEMO with HTTP / Internet / NoAuthentication

VS Code > PowerShell

terraform plan shows No changes after everything settles

 

If terraform plan shows changes despite an apparently complete setup, inspect drift and provider read behavior before applying blindly. The state file records Terraform-managed objects; it does not mean that every entry represents an extra BTP service.

12. Common problems and simple fixes

`terraform` or `btp` is not recognized: Open a fresh terminal; check Windows PATH; verify the install commands completed.

`401 Unauthorized` / password authentication fails: Retry btp login --sso and set USE_BTPCLI_SESSION=true in the same PowerShell session. Current BTP provider SSO uses the CLI session rather than the older deprecated SSO environment variable.

`Subaccount already exists` or duplicate subdomain: The subdomain must be unique in the selected region. Change subaccount_subdomain in terraform.tfvars before the resource has been created.

Entitlement not available: Check the global account entitlement catalog, quotas, plan name and trial region. Some entitlements have already been allocated to the default trial subaccount.

`NOT_SUBSCRIBED` in the output: This often just means an available application plan has not yet been subscribed. Confirm app_name, add the subscription resource and apply. Do not interpret NOT_SUBSCRIBED as a Terraform failure by itself.

Role collection not found: PI_Integration_Developer may not exist until the Cloud Integration capability is active. Finish the browser step, then rerun terraform apply.

Destination 403 or missing: Verify the user's Destination Administrator or suitable subaccount administration rights. Check service enablement and account limitations rather than repeatedly changing the HCL.

`terraform plan` reports no change after editing the file: Make sure the .tf file is in the folder where you run Terraform and is actually saved. Terraform does not read sample files left in the separate steps folder.

Never run `terraform destroy` on an existing subaccount you did not create for this isolated lab. A destroy can remove the subaccount, subscription, destinations and other managed resources. If you choose to clean up this new lab, review the full destroy plan first.

Closing thoughts

This small lab demonstrates why Infrastructure as Code is useful in SAP BTP: a subaccount's core setup becomes readable, reviewable, and repeatable.
