Look at where the "Agent" rows sit. They are at the edges of the process: interpreting demand, explaining approvals, investigating exceptions and analyzing spend. The middle of the process, where money and goods actually move, belongs to integration. The three-way match is the interesting one. The match itself is a rule. The moment it fails, though, someone has to work out why, and that is exactly the kind of work an agent is good at.

So the question is not "agent or integration?" It is "which part of this step needs judgment?"

3. Two layers that work together

Once you accept that split, the architecture becomes cleaner. I think of it as two layers with a governed boundary between them.

The intelligence layer is where agents live, whether they are Joule agents, custom agents built on SAP BTP, or third-party agents. They understand the request, choose the right tools, interpret results, investigate exceptions and recommend or explain the next step.

The execution layer is SAP Integration Suite: Cloud Integration, API Management, Event Mesh, B2B and the connectivity into S/4HANA, ECC and third-party systems. It connects, transforms, routes, retries, secures and monitors.

An agent investigating a blocked invoice should never need to know how to reach the ERP, how to build the payload or which destination to use. It should ask for the evidence through an approved tool and spend its effort on explaining the discrepancy. The integration layer handles the rest.

Figure 1. Agents handle intent and reasoning; SAP Integration Suite provides governed access to business capabilities.

4. Why MCP matters here

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives compatible AI applications a standard way to discover and call tools. That sounds modest, but think about the alternative. Without a standard, every agent project discovers, interprets and rebuilds access to the same backends. The SAP deck compared it to a craftsperson. A good craftsperson is productive because trusted tools are already on the bench before the work starts. Agents need the same thing.

For a procurement agent, the bench might hold a handful of tools:

  • get_purchase_order to retrieve permitted PO details
  • check_approval_status to read the current approval state
  • validate_purchase_order to run defined validations
  • submit_for_approval to start an authorized approval workflow

Each tool has a clear purpose, a typed input and output contract, and narrow permissions. The agent picks the tool. The integration layer does the work.

One caution, because I hear this misunderstanding often: MCP standardizes the conversation between an agent and a tool. It does not make the tool secure, it does not check whether the user has authority to approve, and it does not guarantee the call succeeds. Those controls still live in the gateway, the integration logic and the backend.

5. Design tools for agents, not catalogs for agents

A typical SAP landscape has hundreds of APIs, iFlows and RFCs, many of them overlapping. The instinct is to expose all of them to the agent and let it figure things out. In my experience that is the fastest way to get an agent that is slow, expensive and unpredictable. Large tool catalogs make tool selection ambiguous, and oversized responses fill the context window with noise.

A lesson from one of my own programs: we built an AI assistant that answered purchase-order status questions for procurement and finance users, with a Vertex AI agent sitting behind Apigee X and calling into Ariba. Before it, these questions went into an email queue and often took a day to answer. After it, the answer came back in a few seconds. The model was not what made it work. What made it work was that the agent saw one narrow, well-described capability with a clean response, rather than the raw Ariba API surface. Most of the effort went into the API, not the prompt.

The same thinking applies to composition. Suppose an invoice-investigation agent needs invoice details, PO details and goods-receipt data. The naive design gives it three tools and asks it to correlate the responses. The better design composes them behind one business-oriented interface and returns a focused, structured result.

Figure 2. From multiple APIs to one agent-centric composed API.

This is now something SAP explicitly calls out: combining multiple backend APIs and exposing them as optimized MCP endpoints for agent consumption. The benefits are real (fewer tool calls, less correlation logic in the agent, smaller context, clearer ownership), but they are not free. Composition moves work into the integration layer, and its effect on latency and cost depends on data volumes, caching and how well you handle partial failures. Design it like any other API, with the same care.

The goal is not to expose more APIs to agents. It is to expose better business capabilities.

6. API-centric integration and the API artifact

Anyone who has worked on BTP for a while knows the split. Integration logic (routing, mapping, orchestration) lives in an iFlow in Cloud Integration. Exposure, security policies and throttling live in an API proxy in API Management. Two artifacts, two experiences, two places to look when something breaks.

API-centric integration introduces the API artifact, a single design and runtime element that combines the qualities of both: secure and publish, policy enforcement and throttling on one side; message routing, transformation and call orchestration on the other. It runs on the Integration Cell, a single runtime for Cloud Integration and API Management. According to the session, that removes extra hops and the double charging that came from passing a call through both. Monitoring is unified through the message processing log (MPL), with analytics feeding the existing API Management dashboards.

The capabilities that caught my attention as an architect:

  • Discovery of backend services from BTP destinations, the SAP Gateway catalog service for on-premise S/4HANA, and systems registered in the BTP cockpit's System Landscape.
  • API specifications attached as OpenAPI, or generated from natural language. A machine-readable spec is what lets an API be extended as an MCP tool, so this matters more than it looks.
  • Security with credentials scoped to a controlled set of APIs instead of master credentials, binding to XSUAA for token exchange across BTP, and principal propagation to on-premise systems. Validation of tokens from external OIDC issuers was shown as roadmap.
  • Developer Hub as one catalog where application developers subscribe to APIs and agents discover MCP servers, with self-registration for credentials.

On adoption, SAP's own recommendation was refreshingly conservative: consider the API artifact in the Integration Cell for greenfield projects, with no changes to existing deployments. I would put it this way:

  1. New work: design with the API artifact where the runtime and features you need are available.
  2. Stable integrations: leave them alone. A working iFlow that meets its SLA is not technical debt.
  3. Targeted modernization: consolidate when a flow is already being redesigned, or when a capability needs governed exposure to agents.
  4. Automation later: treat AI-assisted migration as something to evaluate once it is a supported capability, not something to plan budgets around today.

I have led enough migrations, from Oracle SOA 11g to 12c, from SOA to SAP BTP and from Boomi to Apigee X, to say this plainly: mass conversions without a business reason rarely pay back. Modernize where the change already touches.

7. Three paths to MCP with the MCP Gateway

This is the part I think matters most for SAP customers. The MCP Gateway in Integration Suite exposes your APIs, integrations and data sources as governed MCP servers. The session described three alternative starting points. They are options, not sequential steps.

Figure 3. Three paths to MCP enablement with SAP Integration Suite.

Path 1: from an API artifact. Expose a deployed API artifact's operations natively as MCP tools. This is the natural route for new API-centric work.

Path 2: from existing API specifications. Bring in specifications from existing API Management deployments or external HTTP endpoints. The technical spec is translated into MCP schema and enriched with natural-language semantics so agents can understand what each tool does.

Path 3: from RFCs. Expose remote-enabled function modules from ECC or S/4HANA. For a lot of customers this is the big one. Many core processes still run on ECC and on BAPIs that have been stable for fifteen years. Rebuilding every one of them as a new REST service before an agent can use it would delay adoption by years. That said, not every RFC should be agent-callable. Pick them deliberately, scope them tightly, and keep the backend authorization checks in place.

Two other points are worth noting. First, SAP Architecture Center now positions the MCP Gateway as the endorsed pathway for external third-party agents and for customer-built agents on BTP to reach SAP systems, with federation of third-party MCP servers on the roadmap. Second, MCP itself is still evolving quickly. If you run self-managed MCP servers, you own the job of tracking the specification and planning upgrades. A managed gateway takes that off your plate, which is a reasonable trade for most enterprise teams.

8. Guardrails are part of the design, not an add-on

In classic integration, it was usually enough to know that application X called API Y. With agents, you need to know which agent acted, on whose behalf, which tool it called, what authorization applied, and whether the business outcome was what everyone expected. Before any agent touches a transactional system, I want to see answers to these:

  • Identity and least privilege. Which agents and users can call which tools? Scoped credentials, not shared master keys.
  • Business authorization. Technical access must never bypass approval limits or segregation of duties. Being able to call submit_for_approval is not the same as being allowed to approve.
  • Input validation. Validate tool inputs against schema and business constraints before anything executes.
  • Traffic management. Rate limits, IP restrictions and payload protection, so a looping agent cannot flood an ECC system.
  • Error semantics. A rejected PO is a business outcome. An unreachable backend is a technical failure. The agent needs to be able to tell the difference.
  • Traceability. Enough logging to reconstruct a tool call end to end during an incident or an audit.
  • Human oversight. High-value or policy-sensitive actions go to a person. Design that path in from day one.

9. Context engineering is an integration concern

There is a common assumption that more context makes an agent smarter. Usually it does the opposite. Twenty overlapping tools and a 4,000-line payload make it harder for the model to choose correctly, and you pay for every token.

What works is focused tool descriptions, explicit input and output schemas, composed responses that contain only what the task needs, and retrieval on demand rather than up front. Notice that almost all of those are decisions made in the integration layer, not in the prompt. How well an agent behaves depends a great deal on what the surrounding architecture lets it see, reach and do.

10. Putting it together: invoice exception management

Here is how I would apply all of this to a scenario most SAP customers will recognize: thousands of supplier invoices a month, most of which match cleanly and a minority that do not.

Routine invoices never see an agent. Integration Suite ingests them, converts formats, runs the deterministic three-way match and posts them according to the rules. There is no reason to pay for reasoning on an invoice that matches.

Exceptions are where the agent comes in. When the match fails on a price variance, a missing goods receipt or a suspected duplicate, the agent calls a composed get_invoice_context tool, compares the evidence, explains the likely cause in plain language and recommends a next step.

Resolution stays controlled. The agent can trigger an authorized action within its limits or route a recommendation to an AP specialist. Either way, the integration layer validates the request and executes it with the normal controls.

Measurement decides whether it was worth it. I would track exception resolution time, the manual intervention rate, integration failure rate, cost per agent invocation and the share of cases resolved within policy. If those numbers do not move, the agent is a nice demo and nothing more.

11. A word on cost

Agent cost is not just tokens. It includes repeated tool calls, orchestration overhead, monitoring, governance and the time people spend investigating odd behavior. Keeping agents off deterministic steps is the single biggest lever. After that: reuse existing iFlows and APIs, keep responses small, compose where it saves calls, and measure consumption next to business outcomes. Edition requirements and AI-unit terms for these capabilities can change, so confirm current details with SAP before you build a business case.

Closing thoughts: orchestration, not universal agentization

The next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by the biggest model. It will be won by the teams that connect models to business processes without giving up the reliability, security and discipline that integration teams have spent years building.

If you are starting this week, here is what I would do:

  1. Take one end-to-end process, such as P2P, and score each step for reasoning value versus execution value.
  2. Pick one exception-heavy step where an agent clearly helps.
  3. Design two or three narrow, composed tools for it. Not twenty.
  4. Expose them through the MCP Gateway using whichever path fits: API artifact, existing spec or RFC.
  5. Put identity, authorization, rate limits and logging in place before go-live, and measure the outcome.

For those of us who have spent our careers in integration, this is good news. The skills that agentic AI needs most (clean contracts, governed access, reliable execution, good observability) are the ones we already have. Our job is not shrinking. It is moving one layer closer to the business.

I would like to hear how others are approaching this. Are you exposing RFCs to agents, or holding back until APIs are cleaner? Let me know in the comments.

entry.title: Pipeline for Cloud Integration: Exactly Once In Order routing for XI and IDoc inbound processing
entry.content:
In the newest version of the Pipeline for Cloud Integration, we added Exactly Once In Order (EOIO) routing directly into the inbound processing step for both XI and IDoc — the two protocols where ordered delivery matters most in SAP-to-SAP integration. When a message arrives flagged as EOIO, the pipeline detects this at the earliest possible stage and routes it on a dedicated route — bypassing the pipeline steps that are currently incompatible with ordered processing today — and forwards it either to an exclusive JMS queue or a ProcessDirect endpoint. See In Order Handling.

It was a conscious decision not to support EOIO in the pipeline right now as long as we do not support dynamic serialization context which - once supported - will give us much more flexibility in handling EOIO scenarios. So, the current delivery does not cover an End-to-End scenario for EOIO but is a first step to unblock customers that are requiring this and want to use the generic IDoc and Proxy inbound.

You configure the EOIO routes in the Partner Directory for the partner ID representing your configuration scenario. For this, the string parameter InOrderRouteOption has been introduced. As value of the parameter, you need to specify the route option and its specifics. The following options are supported:

  • You route the EOIO messages to an exclusive queue which name is based on the sender context.
  • You route the EOIO messages to an exclusive queue with a name chosen in the Partner Directory.
  • You route the EOIO messages to a ProcessDirect endpoint.

If nothing has been configured, EOIO messages will fail in the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows with custom status ConfigurationOptionNotSupported.

In either case, you need to create an integration flow where you implement the In Order settings on your own. For the ProcessDirect option, you directly send the EOIO message synchronously to the integration flow. When choosing the exclusive queue option, you decouple the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows from your integration flow. By persisting the messages in a JMS queue, Cloud Integration can carry out the retry of the message delivery if there's an error. Because an exclusive JMS queue can have only one consumer at a time, the message sequence can be preserved. See Quality of Service Exactly Once In Order.

In the following, let's go through the different options.

Exclusive queue based on sender context

For XI messages sent with Quality of Service Exactly Once In Order, the XI sender adapter sets the message headers SapQualityOfService equals ExactlyOnceInOrder and SapQueueId holding the queue ID of the incoming message. For the IDoc sender adapter, the message headers SapPlainSoapQoS and SapPlainSoapQueueId are set based on the IDoc control header ARCKEY. Your EOIO messages can then be routed to an exclusive queue with a name provided in the headers SapQueueId and SapPlainSoapQueueId, respectively.

Create an integration flow with an exclusive JMS sender queue. As name for the exclusive JMS sender queue choose the name of the queue ID sent with the message. If different queue IDs are sent, you need to create multiple integration flows. As you can see, this doesn't scale unlimited. So, this only works for quite static queue settings.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ExclusiveQueue:UseSenderContextAsQueue.

Exclusive queue with configured name

Like in the option before, you can use an exclusive JMS queue to decouple the generic XI and IDoc inbound processing flows with from your integration flow. Here, however, you can give the exclusive queue an own name.

Create an integration flow with an exclusive JMS sender queue. As name for the exclusive JMS sender queue choose the configured name, here PIP2EOIO, see below.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ExclusiveQueue:<your chosen queue name>, in this example ExclusiveQueue:PIP2EOIO.

Optionally, because we bypass the rest of the pipeline, in particular the receiver determination, you can create a string parameter receiverDetermination with value equals the receiver system name. Another option would be to create a message header SAP_Receiver in the integration flow holding the receiver system name. This is actually supported for all options, but not shown in the other screenshots.

ProcessDirect option

You can route the EOIO message to an integration flow which you synchronously call via ProcessDirect adapter. In this case, create an integration flow with a ProcessDirect sender adapter.

In the Partner Directory, maintain the partner ID representing the configuration scenario. Create the string parameter InOrderRouteOption with value ProcessDirect:<your chosen ProcessDirect end point>, in this example ProcessDirect:/PIP/Step07/Samples/Scenario_2/EOIO.

 

Special use case: XI to XI route-through

Let's take a look at a special use case. We like to achieve EOIO delivery for a route-through scenario with XI sender and XI receiver, i.e., Point-to-Point without mapping. In this case, we can actually apply the ProcessDirect option whereas as ProcessDirect In Order route we choose the end point of the generic XI outbound processing flow. So, the generic XI inbound processing flow directly calls the generic XI outbound processing flow. The headers SapQualityOfService and SapQueueId are passed through. This ensures that the XI receiver adapter calls the receiver system in Exactly Once In Order mode. Furthermore, dynamic queue IDs are supported. Note, that in this case, the restart in case of a message failure is handled by the sender system.

In the following, we go through the configuration in detail. The colour coding is defined as follows: Green has to do with the landscape staging settings and the partner ID determination, Blue refers to the In Order routing, and Red refers to the XI outbound settings. First of all, we need a partner ID representing the sender system alias with an alternative partner that maps the actual sender business system to the sender system alias. In this case, we assume that we run the scenario in the QA landscape. For an incoming message, the business system is mapped to the alias. Within the pipeline, we work with alias.

Next, for the partner ID representing the configuration scenario we define an alternative partner that maps the sender system alias, the sender interface name and the sender interface namespace to the configuration scenario. This way, we determine the configuration scenario based on the incoming message.

On the String Parameters tab, we define how the configuration scenario is configured. The string parameter receiverDetermination defines the receiver system alias. The InOrderRouteOption defines how we handle the In Order processing. In this case, we opt for the ProcessDirect option. As mentioned above, as address we maintain the end point of the generic XI outbound processing flow. Furthermore, we define the settings of the XI outbound processing, in this case the receiver interface name and its namespace. See XI Receiver Adapter.

For the receiver system alias, we also need to define an alternative partner that maps the actual receiver business system to the receiver system alias. Before we send out the message to the receiver, we map the alias to the corresponding business system.

For configuring the XI connection parameters, we support different options. In our case, we use the Partner Directory option. For this, we create a partner ID representing the actual receiver business system and maintain the configuration parameters. i.e., proxy type, authentication type, credential name, and XI end point of the receiver system. For a complete list of configuration options, see XI Receiver Adapter.

If you run the scenario, you should see two message processing logs in the message monitor belonging to one message exchange. As you can see, the message has been routed through and delivered via Exactly Once In Order.

The options outlined here are initial steps to realize EOIO extending the generic XI and IDoc pipeline steps. We are looking into options to realize the E2E scenario using Exclusive Queue but also the planned "Support many serialization contexts for parallel exactly once in order processing (EOIO)" via the pipeline. Therefore, please stay tuned for further updates of the pipeline package.

entry.title: iFlow Transport with Git and CI/CD – Setting Externalized Parameters with Automation Pilot
entry.content:
Introduction

Here are two recent updates around Cloud Integration:

  • July 2026: Cloud Integration can push iFlows to a Git repository and pull them from it.
  • September 2026: SAP Automation Pilot introduced the SAP Integration Suite (is-sapcp) catalog. It manages the lifecycle of iFlows, externalized parameters and the Partner Directory.

In addition, SAP Continuous Integration and Delivery (CI/CD) provides the SAP Integration Suite Artifacts 2.0 job. It takes an iFlow from a Git repository, uploads it to a target tenant and deploys it.

A possible next step would be to combine them: push an iFlow to Git, transport it to the target tenant with CI/CD, and then set the externalized parameters for that environment with Automation Pilot.

So I tried it. In this blog post, I will show how I connected these services and which gaps I had to bridge.

Note: I tested this on a BTP trial account. It is not a production-proven procedure.

Architecture

Figure: Overall architecture

  1. Develop the iFlow in the Dev tenant and push it to GitHub.
  2. Run the CI/CD job. It uploads the iFlow to the target tenant and deploys it.
  3. When the job succeeds, Alert Notification triggers an Automation Pilot command. The command sets the externalized parameters for the target environment and deploys them.

CI/CD deploys the iFlow, and Automation Pilot deploys only the externalized parameters.

Bridging the gaps

Gap 1: Repository structure

When Cloud Integration pushes an iFlow, it creates a folder named after the iFlow ID, so one repository can hold several iFlows. The CI/CD job, however, expects the content of one iFlow at the repository root.

# Pushed by Cloud Integration   # Expected by CI/CD
Test_Flow/                       META-INF/
├── META-INF/                    src/
├── src/                         metainfo.prop
└── metainfo.prop

As-is, the Upload stage fails with Integration flow project must contain a manifest file. The fix is one additional command in the Upload stage (Additional Commands > Run First in Stage). It zips the iFlow folder into the package.zip that the stage uploads:

python3 -c "import shutil; shutil.make_archive('package','zip','<iFlow ID>')"

Figure: Additional command in the Upload stage

Gap 2: Passing externalized parameters to Automation Pilot

The Automation Pilot command BulkPromoteIFlowToEnvironment takes the iFlow ID (iflowId) and the externalized parameters to set in the target environment (iflowParameters). The CI/CD Build Notification can carry such values in its Custom Tag:

Figure: Custom tag in the Build Notification settings

When Alert Notification triggers Automation Pilot, though, the whole event goes to the command as one input. The following JSON is the event (abbreviated). The custom tag is nested inside it as a JSON string:

{
  "eventType": "build.end",
  "subject": "Build has finished with 'SUCCESS'",
  "tags": {
    "cicd:custom": "{\"iflowId\": \"Test_Flow\", \"iflowParameters\": [{\"key\":\"header1\",\"value\":\"bulk\"}]}",
    "cicd:issuer": "SAP Continuous Integration and Delivery",
    "cicd:stage": "Integration Flow Result",
    ...
  },
  "resource": { "resourceType": "SAP Integration Suite Artifacts", ... },
  ...
}

So I created a small wrapper command, PromoteIFlowFromAnsEvent, with the help of SAP Automation Pilot Agent Skills. It receives the whole event as its payload input and runs two steps:

  1. customTag reads the cicd:custom tag from the event. If the tag has no iflowId, the command stops with an error message.
  2. promote calls BulkPromoteIFlowToEnvironment. It takes iflowId and iflowParameters from the custom tag (see the red boxes in the figure below), and the connection details of the target tenant from the command's input.

Figure: The promote step of the wrapper command

You can import the command from GitHub: https://github.com/miyasuta/automation-pilot-cicd-iflow

Configuration

Prerequisites:

  • A GitHub repository and a personal access token (PAT)
  • The following services in your subaccount:
    • SAP Integration Suite
    • SAP Continuous Integration and Delivery
    • SAP Alert Notification service
    • SAP Automation Pilot

1. Cloud Integration

Connect the repository and push the iFlow. See Integrating with GitHub and this blog post.

2. CI/CD

Set up an Integration Suite Artifacts 2.0 job as described in the documentation. Notes:

  • Create the integration package in the target tenant beforehand. CI/CD does not create it.
  • For Design Time Authentication, use a service key of SAP Process Integration Runtime (plan api) in the target subaccount.
  • Additional settings for this scenario:
    • Upload > Additional Commands > Run First in Stage: Enter the zip command (Gap 1)
    • Build Notification: Turn on the notification, and enter the Alert Notification service key and the custom tag (Gap 2)

3. Automation Pilot

This step assumes that the wrapper command (Gap 2) already exists in your Automation Pilot tenant.

  1. Create an Input with the target tenant's credentials (clientId, clientSecret, tokenUrl, apiHost) from a service key of SAP Process Integration Runtime (plan api).
  2. In Executions, click Build Event Trigger. Select the command and the input. On the Mapping tab, map the event to payload. Copy the event trigger URL.

Figure: Build Event Trigger, General tab

Figure: Build Event Trigger, Mapping tab

The SAP Process Integration Runtime (plan api) service instances used by CI/CD and Automation Pilot have the following roles:

RoleCI/CDAutomation Pilot
WorkspacePackagesEdit✓✓
WorkspaceArtifactsDeploy✓✓
MonitoringDataRead✓✓
WorkspacePackagesConfigure ✓

Automation Pilot additionally needs WorkspacePackagesConfigure to update the externalized parameters.

4. Alert Notification

In Alert Notification, configure the following so that a successful CI/CD build triggers the Automation Pilot command:

  • Action: Create an action that calls the event trigger URL. Enter the username and password for the event trigger.
  • Conditions: Create two conditions so that only successful builds trigger the command: eventType equals build.end, and subject contains SUCCESS. For details of the event, see the event reference.
  • Subscription: Create a subscription that combines the action and both conditions.

Result

I ran the CI/CD job, and it finished successfully:

Figure: Successful CI/CD build

Alert Notification triggered the command:

Figure: Command execution in Automation Pilot

The externalized parameter has the value from the custom tag:

Figure: Externalized parameter set in the target tenant

Considerations

  • Single iFlows only. Both the Git integration and the CI/CD job handle individual iFlows. Scripts, value mappings and other artifacts in the package are not transported. If the iFlow depends on them, import the package to the target first.
  • One CI/CD job per iFlow and target environment. The number of jobs grows with the number of iFlows and environments. This setup can be an option for two-tier landscapes or a small number of iFlows. Otherwise, the standard approach is Cloud Transport Management with Content Assembly Service.

Summary

These services work well together. Only two small gaps had to be bridged: an additional zip command for the repository structure, and a wrapper command that extracts the externalized parameters from the Alert Notification event. With those, a single run of the CI/CD job transports an iFlow and sets its environment-specific parameters.

entry.title: The Utility Flows Deep Dive — Part 3
entry.content:
The Utility Flows Deep Dive — Part 3

Hey, We're Almost Done!

So if you've been following along, you now have:

  • A main integration flow that does actual business work (writes to SFTP in our example)
  • An Exception Handling flow that orchestrates error handling with three sequential calls
  • An AI Utility flow that converts ugly technical errors into human-readable messages
  • A universal JSON payload structure that feeds multiple downstream systems

But we haven't talked much about the actual utility flows that receive this enriched data. You know, the ones that create ServiceNow tickets and send logs to Loggly?

That's what Part 3 is all about.

What We're Covering Today

Let me be straight with you:

  • ServiceNow Utility Flow: How it extracts the serviceNow section and creates tickets
  • Loggly Utility Flow: How one flow handles both INFO and ERROR logs
  • Testing the whole thing: Using Postman to make stuff break
  • Reading the traces: What to look for when debugging
  • Go-live checklist: The stuff I wish someone had told me before deploying

Grab some coffee. Let's finish this.

ServiceNow Utility Flow — Creating Tickets That Actually Help

 

Alright, so the Exception Handling flow calls this utility with that beautiful universal JSON payload. This flow's job is simple: extract the ServiceNow-specific section and create an incident ticket.

The Flow Structure

Address: /AI_Exception_Loggly_Accelerator/Service_Now_Utility_Flow/

Here's what happens:

  1. ProcessDirect Sender — Receives the universal JSON from Exception Handling flow
  2. Groovy Script (GS_Ticket) — Extracts just the serviceNow section
  3. Request-Reply (RR_ServiceNow) — Calls ServiceNow REST API
  4. End Event — Returns success to Exception Handling flow

The Groovy Script Magic

The GS_Ticket script is actually pretty straightforward:

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message
import groovy.json.JsonSlurper
import groovy.json.JsonOutput

def Message processData(Message message) {
    // Parse the universal JSON
    def jsonPayload = new JsonSlurper().parseText(message.getBody(String))
    
    // Extract ONLY the serviceNow section
    def serviceNowData = jsonPayload.serviceNow
    
    // Map to ServiceNow's expected format
    def incidentData = [
        short_description: serviceNowData.shortDescription,
        description: serviceNowData.description,
        impact: serviceNowData.impact,
        urgency: serviceNowData.urgency
    ]
    
    message.setBody(JsonOutput.toJson(incidentData))
    return message
}

What this does:

  • Receives: Full JSON with errorDetails, serviceNow, and loggly sections
  • Extracts: Only the serviceNow section
  • Outputs: Clean JSON ready for ServiceNow API

No need to transform the entire payload. Just grab what you need.

The ServiceNow REST Adapter

The Request-Reply step uses an HTTP adapter configured for ServiceNow:

  • Method: POST
  • Endpoint: https://dev211719.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident
  • Authentication: Basic Auth (stored in Security Material)
  • Headers: Content-Type: application/json

ServiceNow responds with the created ticket number, which we... honestly just ignore. We got what we needed — the ticket was created.

The Exception Subprocess

Yeah, even the ServiceNow utility has an exception handler. See that exception subprocess at the bottom?

Error Start Event → Process Call (Local Integration Process) → Escalate End Event

Why? If ServiceNow is down (or slow, or returning 500 errors), we don't want the entire Exception Handling flow to crash. The Escalate End Event lets the Exception Handling flow continue to the next step (calling Loggly).

Think about it:

  • ServiceNow fails → Escalate End catches it
  • Exception Handling flow continues
  • Loggly still gets the log
  • At least you have SOME record of the error

Without this, one system being down would block the entire error handling chain. Not good.

Loggly Utility Flow — The Unified Logger

 

This one's interesting because it handles both INFO and ERROR logs with the same flow. Remember in Part 2 when I mentioned the main flow logs successful messages? It uses this same Loggly utility.

Address: /AI_Exception_Loggly_Accelerator/Loggly_Utility_Flow/

How It Works

  1. ProcessDirect Sender — Receives either:
    • Universal JSON (from Exception Handling flow during errors)
    • Simple info message (from Main flow during success)
  2. Groovy Script (GS_Info_Error) — Checks the logLevel property
  3. Content Modifier (CM_Headers_Declare) — Sets HTTP headers
  4. HTTP Adapter — Sends to Loggly endpoint
  5. End Event — Done

The Smart Groovy Script

The GS_Info_Error script does some simple logic:

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message
import groovy.json.JsonSlurper

def Message processData(Message message) {
    def properties = message.getProperties()
    def logLevel = properties.get("logLevel") ?: "INFO"
    
    def jsonPayload = new JsonSlurper().parseText(message.getBody(String))
    
    if (logLevel == "ERROR") {
        // Extract loggly section from universal JSON
        def logglyData = jsonPayload.loggly
        message.setBody(JsonOutput.toJson(logglyData))
    } else {
        // Keep the entire payload for INFO logs
        // (it's already in the right format)
    }
    
    return message
}

The logic:

  • If logLevel=ERROR property exists → Extract just the loggly section
  • If no property (defaults to INFO) → Send the whole payload as-is

The HTTP Adapter

The actual Loggly configuration:

  • URL: https://logs-01.loggly.com/inputs/<YOUR_TOKEN>/tag/SAP_CPI/
  • Method: POST
  • Headers:
    • Content-Type: application/json
    • Authorization: bearer <token> (stored in secure parameters)

Loggly receives structured JSON it can search, filter, and alert on. Way better than plain text logs.

The Exception Subprocess (Again)

Same pattern:

Error Start Event → Process Call (Local Integration Process) → Escalate End Event

Why? If Loggly is down, we still want the Exception Handling flow to complete successfully. The main flow shouldn't crash just because our logging endpoint is unreachable.

The beauty of this design:

  • ServiceNow fails? → Loggly still logs it
  • Loggly fails? → ServiceNow ticket still created
  • Both fail? → At least the main flow returns 200 to the sender

Testing the Whole Thing (Please Don't Skip This)

Happy Path Testing with Postman

First, let's make sure everything works when there are NO errors:

  1. Fire up Postman and create a POST request
  2. URL: Your SAP CPI endpoint (something like https://your-tenant.it-cpi01.cfapps.eu10-001.hana.ondemand.com/http/exceptionlogglyutility)
  3. Body: A valid XML or JSON payload (whatever your main flow expects)
  4. Send it

What should happen:

  • You get HTTP 200 back
  • File appears on SFTP server
  • Loggly shows an INFO-level log entry
  • No ServiceNow ticket (because nothing failed)

If this doesn't work, don't even bother testing the error handling yet. Fix the happy path first.

Sad Path Testing (Make Things Break)

Now comes the fun part. We're going to break stuff on purpose:

Test 1: SFTP Connection Failure

  1. Go to your Main Integration Flow
  2. Change the SFTP hostname to something wrong (sftp.example.com or whatever)
  3. Deploy the flow
  4. Send the same Postman request

Expected results:

  • HTTP 200 response (yes, still success!)
  • SFTP write fails (obviously)
  • Exception Handling flow triggers
  • AI Utility classifies as SFTP error (instant, 200ms)
  • ServiceNow ticket created with "Failed to connect to SFTP server"
  • Loggly logs the error with full details

Test 2: Trigger Gemini API Call

How do you test the 10% case where Gemini actually gets called?

  1. Add a Content Modifier in the main flow that throws a weird error:
    throw new Exception("SUPER_RARE_ERROR_12345_UNKNOWN")
  2. Deploy and test

Expected results:

  • AI Utility's instant classifier doesn't recognize it
  • Falls back to Gemini API (takes 2-5 seconds)
  • Gemini analyzes and responds with custom error message
  • Rest of the flow proceeds normally

Viewing Traces

This shows the main flow execution with the exception subprocess being triggered.

This shows the sequential calls to AI Utility, ServiceNow, and Loggly.

This shows the AI processing (instant classification or Gemini API call).

This confirms the incident ticket was created successfully.

This confirms the log was sent to Loggly.

ServiceNow Incident Ticket

Check your ServiceNow instance to see the created incident with AI-enriched description.

Inspect the full ticket details to verify all fields were populated correctly.

Loggly Info and Error Logs

Simulating Failures (The Important Part)

Look, I know testing failures isn't fun. But trust me, you do NOT want to discover your error handling doesn't work when there's an actual production issue at 2 AM.

Here's how I test the safety nets:

Scenario 1: AI Utility Fails

How to trigger:

  1. Go to AI Utility Flow
  2. Find the Groovy script (GS_Gemini_API_Call)
  3. Add this at the top: throw new Exception("Testing AI failure")
  4. Deploy
  5. Trigger an error in the main flow

What should happen:

  • AI Utility's exception subprocess catches it
  • Escalate End Event triggers
  • Exception Handling flow continues anyway
  • ServiceNow and Loggly get called with the RAW error (not ideal, but better than nothing)
  • Main flow still returns HTTP 200

Scenario 2: ServiceNow Is Down

How to trigger:

  1. Go to ServiceNow Utility Flow
  2. Change the REST adapter URL to something invalid (https://fake.service-now.com)
  3. Deploy
  4. Trigger an error in the main flow

What should happen:

  • AI Utility enriches the error (works fine)
  • ServiceNow call fails (HTTP connection error)
  • ServiceNow utility's exception subprocess catches it
  • Escalate End Event triggers
  • Exception Handling flow continues to Loggly
  • Loggly logs the error successfully
  • Main flow returns HTTP 200
  • Result: No ServiceNow ticket, but at least Loggly has the log

Scenario 3: Loggly Endpoint Unreachable

How to trigger:

  1. Go to Loggly Utility Flow
  2. Change the HTTP adapter URL to something invalid
  3. Deploy
  4. Trigger an error

What should happen:

  • AI Utility enriches the error
  • ServiceNow ticket created successfully
  • Loggly call fails
  • Loggly utility's exception subprocess catches it
  • Escalate End Event triggers
  • Exception Handling flow completes
  • Main flow returns HTTP 200
  • Result: ServiceNow ticket exists, but no Loggly log

Scenario 4: Everything Fails (Worst Case)

How to trigger: Break ALL the utility flows (bad URLs, throw exceptions, whatever).

What should happen:

  • Each utility flow's Escalate End catches its own failure
  • Exception Handling flow completes all three calls (they all fail gracefully)
  • Main flow returns HTTP 200
  • Result: No notifications anywhere, BUT the sender doesn't get an error

This is the "everything is on fire but at least we're not blocking the business" scenario.

Why This Matters

Without Escalate End Events:

  • One utility fails → entire Exception Handling flow crashes
  • Exception Handling flow crashes → main flow returns HTTP 500
  • Sender system sees failure → might retry infinitely
  • Your integration is now a broken mess

With Escalate End Events:

  • One utility fails → it's contained
  • Other utilities still run
  • Main flow completes normally
  • Sender is happy
  • You fix the broken utility when you get to the office (not at 2 AM)

Go-Live Checklist (Don't Deploy Without This)

Before you even THINK about deploying this to production, go through this list:

Security

  • [ ] API keys in Secure Parameters, not hardcoded in Groovy scripts
  • [ ] SFTP credentials in Security Material, not in adapter config
  • [ ] ServiceNow credentials in Security Material
  • [ ] Loggly token externalized (don't commit it to Git)
  • [ ] All passwords rotated if they were ever in plain text during testing

Architecture

  • [ ] Escalate End Events in all utility flows (AI, ServiceNow, Loggly)
  • [ ] Exception Subprocesses have Error Start Events (not regular Start Events)
  • [ ] ProcessDirect addresses match exactly (check for trailing slashes)
  • [ ] Sequential calls in Exception Handling flow (AI → ServiceNow → Loggly)

Logging and Monitoring

  • [ ] Message logging enabled on all flows (you'll need this when debugging)
  • [ ] Log attachments stored for at least 30 days
  • [ ] Loggly searches configured to alert on ERROR level
  • [ ] ServiceNow assignment group set correctly

Testing

  • [ ] Happy path tested (normal message processes successfully)
  • [ ] SFTP failure tested (instant classifier works)
  • [ ] Unknown error tested (Gemini API fallback works)
  • [ ] ServiceNow down tested (Escalate End allows flow to continue)
  • [ ] Loggly down tested (Escalate End allows flow to continue)

Performance

  • [ ] Instant classifier handles 90%+ of errors (check AI Utility traces)
  • [ ] Gemini response time < 5 seconds (check AI Utility traces for Gemini calls)
  • [ ] Exception handling adds < 5 seconds to total flow time
  • [ ] No rate limiting issues with Gemini API (test with burst of errors)

If you can check all these boxes, you're ready to go live. If not... well, you know what to do.

Final Thoughts

So that's it. Three parts, a bunch of screenshots, and probably way more detail than you asked for.

But here's the thing: this architecture works. I've seen it handle thousands of errors in production. The instant classifier saves money on API calls. The Escalate End Events prevent cascading failures. The universal JSON payload makes it easy to add new destinations.

Is it perfect? No. Could you simplify it? Probably. But when something breaks at 3 AM and you're still in bed because the error handling did its job? That's when you'll appreciate the extra effort.

What You've Built

Let's recap:

✅ Main Integration Flow — Does business work, delegates errors
✅ Exception Handling Flow — Orchestrates three sequential utility calls
✅ AI Utility Flow — Classifies 90% of errors instantly, calls Gemini for weird ones
✅ ServiceNow Utility Flow — Creates tickets with human-friendly descriptions
✅ Loggly Utility Flow — Logs both INFO and ERROR messages
✅ Escalate End Events — Prevent one failure from breaking everything
✅ Universal JSON Payload — One structure, multiple destinations

What's Next for You?

Here are some ideas if you want to extend this:

  • Add Slack notifications (extract a slack section from the universal payload)
  • Add retry logic in the utility flows (with exponential backoff)
  • Enhance the instant classifier with your environment's specific errors
  • Add metrics (count errors by type, track Gemini vs instant classification ratio)
  • Create a dashboard in Loggly showing top errors

The architecture supports all of this because we built it with extensibility in mind.

Summary

You now have:

  • A reliable integration that never loses the main payload
  • An AI-powered utility with instant error classification (90% of errors in 200ms)
  • Sequential exception handling that enriches errors before logging
  • ServiceNow incident creation with human-friendly descriptions
  • Centralized Loggly logging with structured JSON
  • Escalate End Events that prevent cascading failures
  • A testing recipe to keep everything trustworthy over time

Thanks for sticking with this series! If you adapt these flows for your own tenant, let me know how it goes or what you changed. Seriously, drop a comment. I'd love to hear about your use cases.

Now go build something that fails gracefully.

Questions? Feedback? Found a bug in my logic? Hit me up in the comments. I'll respond when I'm not debugging ProcessDirect addressing issues.

entry.title: Updating SmartRecruiters Job Fields via API When Position Mapping Is Not Available
entry.content:
The API-Based Workaround

SmartRecruiters exposes a public REST API that allows all five fields to be updated programmatically on any existing job. The workaround design has four steps:

Step 1: Job Created in SmartRecruiters

A job is created (manually, from a Position, or via integration). SmartRecruiters fires the job.created webhook event containing the new job's ID.

Step 2: Webhook Receives the Event

An integration middleware (SAP Integration Suite, BTP, or any HTTP listener) receives the job.created event payload and extracts the job ID.

Step 3: Enrich with Source Data

The middleware looks up the correct values for Industry, Function, Experience Level, Type of Employment, and Location from the source Position or a mapping table.

Step 4: PATCH the Job via SmartRecruiters API

A JSON PATCH call is sent to https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId} with all five field updates in a single request.

API Call Details

PATCH  https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId}

[
  {
    "path": "/industry",
    "op": "add",
    "value": { "id": "airlines_aviation" }
  },
  {
    "path": "/function",
    "op": "add",
    "value": { "id": "administrative" }
  },
  {
    "path": "/experienceLevel",
    "op": "add",
    "value": { "id": "director" }
  },
  {
    "path": "/typeOfEmployment",
    "op": "add",
    "value": { "id": "permanent" }
  },
  {
    "path": "/location",
    "op": "add",
    "value": {
      "countryCode": "us",
      "regionCode": "CA",
      "city": "San Francisco"
    }
  }
]

Tip: Use the SmartRecruiters GET /industries, /functions, /experience-levels, and /types-of-employment endpoints to retrieve all valid picklist IDs for your tenant.

https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/docs/industries

https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/docs/functions

https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/docs/levels

https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/docs/typesofemployment

Screenshot — PATCH Call in API Client

The screenshot below shows the PATCH request body and the 200 OK response returned by the SmartRecruiters API:

Triggering the Integration via Webhook

To make this workaround fully automated, configure a webhook subscription in SmartRecruiters to fire whenever a new job is created. The recommended event is:

Webhook Event:  job.created

The webhook payload includes the job id, which your middleware can immediately use to fire the PATCH call. The screenshot below shows a sample job.created webhook event:

Webhook Configuration Tips

  • Subscribe to job.created in the SmartRecruiters Admin panel under Integrations → Webhooks.
  • Your endpoint should respond with HTTP 200 within the timeout window to acknowledge receipt.
  • Implement idempotency — store processed job IDs to avoid duplicate PATCH calls if the webhook retries.
  • Use GET /jobs/{jobId} to check whether the fields are already set before calling PATCH, to handle re-fires gracefully.
  • This integration can be built on SAP Integration Suite, SAP BTP, or any HTTP-capable middleware.
    Summary -  
  • KBA 3746432 documents that Location, Function, Industry, Experience Level, and Type of Employment cannot currently be mapped from a Position in SmartRecruiters.
  • Manual workaround (without API): Recruiters must manually populate these fields for every job.
  • API solution: A single JSON PATCH call to https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId} updates all five fields in one request.
  • Automation trigger: Subscribe to the job.created webhook to fire the PATCH call automatically whenever a new job is created — eliminating manual intervention entirely.

entry.title: New Pattern: Migrating Content-Based Routing Synchronous Scenarios to SAP IS using Migration Tool
entry.content:
This blog post is part of the series Master Blog: SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration – Tool and Guidance . In this edition, we focus specifically on migrating Content-Based Routing (CBR) Synchronous Scenarios to SAP Integration Suite using the Migration Tool.  

What This Blog Covers

The Migration Tool in SAP Integration Suite now supports CBR Synchronous scenarios. This post walks you through everything you need to migrate one: 

  • What makes a CBR scenario synchronous  and the one constraint that sets it apart from async CBR 
  • The eight supported CBR Standard Synchronous cases, broken down by operations, receivers, and interfaces 
  • How the Migration Tool detects the pattern from your ICO automatically 
  • What the Standard Approach generates, and where it differs from the async migration 
  • How the Pipeline Approach works : the three flows, the Partner Directory, and the receiverDetermination XSLT 
  • What to check before you go live

Understanding Synchronous Content-Based Routing in SAP PO 

In a Content-Based Routing scenario, a message does not arrive with a fixed destination. The runtime inspects the message payload, evaluates it against the conditions defined in Receiver Determination, and selects the receiver at that moment. The routing is governed entirely by the content of the message: a field value, an element, or a structure within the payload. 

In practice, this means the following: 

  • Several receivers are configured, and each is associated with its own routing condition. 
  • The decision is dynamic. The same configuration can deliver different messages to different systems according to their content. 
  • A receiver may require the message in a specific format. Through Interface Determination, the same incoming message can be mapped differently depending on which receiver is selected. 

If you are new to Content-Based Routing (CBR) in SAP PO, we recommend first reading our earlier blog Migrating Content-Based Routing Scenarios Using th... - SAP Community  which explains how CBR works, including Receiver Determination and Interface Determination in detail. 

On top of everything CBR already does, the synchronous variant adds one thing: the sender waits for a response.

What Makes it Synchronous? 

Three things together define this as a synchronous scenario: 

  • Both sides use synchronous interfaces

             In SAP PO, a synchronous service interface defines both a request message and a corresponding response message. It's a two-way contract from the start something goes in, something comes back. An asynchronous interface only defines one direction. 

  • Two-Directional Message Mappings

             Because the sender and receiver typically have different formats, two mappings are required:

  •     Request Mapping : transforms the sender's payload into the format the receiver expects 
  •     Response Mapping : transforms the receiver's reply into the format the sender expects 
  • The Connection Stays Open 

             The sender sends the message and waits. It doesn't move on until a reply comes back on the same connection. If something  goes wrong such as a routing issue, a mapping failure, a timeout the sender still needs an answer. Even if it's an error, the caller is waiting. 

            One rule that changes everything 

             In asynchronous CBR, you can route to multiple receivers at once, each gets their own copy. Synchronous doesn't work that way. The sender is waiting for one response, so the routing must land on exactly one receiver and one interface. This means your routing conditions need to be set up so only one can ever match at a time. If two conditions match the same message, things break. If none match, the scenario must throw an error because the sender hasn't moved on yet and is still waiting for a reply. 

Migration of CBR synchronous scenarios using Standard approach and Pipeline approach 

Supported Scenarios in CBR Standard Synchronous 

Every one of these uses a Local Rule with XPath for the routing conditions. 

One thing to keep in mind: when you have N receivers, each one needs its own routing condition, otherwise the scenario isn't valid.

Standard Synchronous Scenario in SAP PO 

 The scenario covered in this blog involves an ICO (Integration Configuration Object) with: 

  • Multiple receivers, each with its own receiver interface 
  • Routing conditions defined per receiver 
  • Standard Receiver Determination Type (operation-specific) 
  • Both Receiver Determination and Interface Determination configured 

This represents one of the more complex real-world setups in SAP PO and the Migration Tool handles it end to end. 

Receiver Determination 

 

Interface Determination 

Picking the Right Pattern in the Migration Wizard 

In Step 3 where you have to Choose Pattern and Approach, the Migration Tool automatically detects the pattern based on your ICO configuration and presents Content-Based Routing Synchronous as the predefined migration pattern.  

At this step, you also select your approach: Standard or Pipeline. 

Standard Approach 

The Standard Approach for CBR synchronous migration follows the same structural pattern as the asynchronous CBR migration. For a full walkthrough of the inbound routing logic, Receiver Determination, Interface Determination, and outbound delivery refer to blog Migrating Content-Based Routing Scenarios Using th... - SAP Community. Below, we focus on what is specific to the synchronous pattern. 

Key Differences in the Synchronous Pattern 

  • Inbound Flow uses ProcessDirect Instead of JMS 

  This is the most fundamental infrastructure difference between the two patterns: 

 

Asynchronous CBR 

Synchronous CBR 

Adapter used 

JMS 

ProcessDirect 

Communication model 

Fire-and-forget . Message is queued 

Request-Reply 

Inbound flow behavior 

Hands off the message and exits 

Waits for a response before returning to sender 

In asynchronous CBR, the inbound flow hands the message to a JMS queue and its job is done. In the synchronous pattern, JMS cannot be used, it is a one-way, queue-based mechanism with no return path. Instead, the inbound flow uses a ProcessDirect adapter with a Request Reply step to call the next flow directly and stays connected until a response comes back. That response is then returned to the sender on the same channel. 

  • Routing must land on exactly one receiver 

The Groovy script evaluates conditions the same way it does in async CBR. The difference is what happens with the result in synchronous; it must resolve to exactly one receiver and one interface. You can't route to two receivers at once because there's only one connection open and one response expected. 

If two conditions match the same message, the behavior is unpredictable. If none match, the flow must throw an error because the sender is still waiting for a reply. 

  • The outbound flow also sends a response back 

In asynchronous CBR, the outbound flow delivers the request and is done. In the synchronous pattern, it has to do the return trip too: 

Direction 

What Happens 

Request 

Routes using the SAP_Receiver header, applies the request mapping, delivers to the receiver 

Response 

Gets the reply back, applies the response mapping, cleans up internal headers, and returns it to the sender 

Without the response mapping and the header cleanup, the response never makes it back cleanly. Both steps matter.

Pipeline Approach 

This section demonstrates the Pipeline Approach for migrating the same scenario. A pipeline represents the complete set of processing steps for a message. It consists of a set of pipeline elements that call pipeline services - for example, carrying out mappings or routing messages to different receivers. 

Before going further, we recommend reading Introducing the new pipeline concept in Cloud Inte... - SAP Community which takes us through the basics of pipeline concept.

For a deeper understanding of the Pipeline Approach, please refer to the following references: 

Migration Tooling now supporting migration via the pipeline approach 

Applying the pipeline concept for an integration scenario in general 

Learn here the differences and characteristics of each approach to choose the one that aligns best with your migration needs Standard vs Pipeline Approach

 

Key Highlights in the Migration Wizard for Pipeline Approach 

Once the Pipeline Approach is selected in Step 3, the Migration Tool enables you to: 

  • Review and adjust alternative partner details if needed before anything is finalized 
  • Verify or update receiver and interface conditions that were migrated from SAP PO, if needed 

This review step is your safety net, catch anything that needs adjusting before the artifacts are generated. 

What Gets Generated After a Successful Migration 

Once the migration completes, the tool presents a full overview of all generated artifacts.  

On the first tab, you can see all three integration flows that were created, one scenario-specific inbound flow and two scenario-specific outbound flows (one per receiver-interface combination). Clicking the View Artifact button navigates you directly to each flow in Cloud Integration.

The PID and Its Parameters 

A Partner ID (PID) is created along with all associated configuration parameters. The Partner Directory tab gives you a structured view of everything that was generated and how it's connected together. 

For a deeper dive into how the Partner Directory works within the Pipeline concept, refer to: Using the Partner Directory in the Pipeline Concept 

 

The receiverDetermination Binary Parameter — Where Your Routing Lives 

Inside the Binary Parameters tab, a parameter named receiverDetermination is automatically created with an XSL content type. 

This is the one that does all the routing work at runtime. It contains the XSLT logic that reads your incoming message and decides which receiver gets it. Think of it as your CBR routing conditions — just packaged as an XSLT and stored in the Partner Directory instead of sitting inside the flow.  

A look at the generated XSLT 

 

The XSLT evaluates XPath expressions against the incoming message content to determine the appropriate receiver and interface. Here is how the routing logic looks: 

Condition 1: 

<xsl:if test="(/p1:MT_JOAH_Employee_REQ/Employee/FirstName = 'Marina')"> 

If FirstName is Marina, then the message is routed to receiver BC_PIELE_Receiver_2 and interface /Demo_CBR_Sync_pip_Blog/pip07/BC_PIELE_Receiver_2/IFIndex1 is called. 

Condition 2: 

<xsl:if test="(/p1:MT_JOAH_Employee_REQ/Employee/FirstName = 'John')"> 

If FirstName is John, then the message is routed to receiver BC_PIELE_Receiver and interface /Demo_CBR_Sync_pip_Blog/pip07/BC_PIELE_Receiver/IFIndex1 is called. 

And if nothing matches? The message isn't quietly dropped. The XSLT raises an error, so nothing gets misrouted. 

Integration Flow in Cloud Integration 

Inbound Integration Process (Scenario-Specific) 

 

 

 

This is where the message enters the pipeline. The sender adapter receives it, and the flow sets three headers: SAP_Sender, SAP_SenderInterface, and SAP_MessageType  which drive everything that follows. If the message needs format conversion before it goes further (JSON to XML, for example), a local subprocess takes care of that first. 

From there, the flow calls the generic synchronous runtime using a ProcessDirect adapter with a Request Reply step  and waits. When the response comes back, it can convert the format again if needed (XML to JSON), cleans up the pipeline headers, and returns the response to the sender. If anything fails at any point, an Exception SubProcess steps in and sends a structured error back  so the caller always gets a reply, success or failure. 

Integrated Messaging Runtime Sync (Generic) 

 

This is the second flow : Pipeline v2 Generic Step02 - Integrated Messaging Runtime Sync, available in the Cloud Integration Pipeline – Generic Pipelines package under Discover → Integrations. 

The important thing about this flow: it's shared. You deploy it once and every sync scenario uses it. It's called directly by the inbound flow via ProcessDirect and handles the central runtime logic for synchronous message processing. 

To explore the full details of how synchronous scenarios work within the Pipeline concept, check out the official SAP documentation: Integrated Messaging Runtime (Synchronous) | SAP Help Portal 

Outbound Processing (Scenario-Specific) 

 

 

 

This is the third flow  and in our scenario there are two of them, one per receiver-interface combination. Each outbound flow handles one receiver: it maps the request into the receiver's format, delivers it via a Request Reply step, maps the response back, and passes it upstream. 

One outbound flow per receiver-interface combination, so if you have three receivers with two interfaces each, expect six outbound flows in total. 

 Post-Migration Checklist - What to Verify Before You Go Live 

A successful migration isn't a green light to deploy. Run your checks first. 

For Post-Migration activities, after successfully migrating CBR Integration flow, please refer to the section Post-Migration Activities – Key Points to Keep in Mind 

For other manual activities for specific scenarios, please refer to the section “Manual Activities Depending on Integration Scenario” the P2P Blog from series 

 Wrapping up 

Migrating a Content-Based Routing Synchronous scenario from SAP PO to SAP Integration Suite involves more than moving artifacts, it requires understanding the two-way communication model, ensuring the correct request and response mappings are in place, and verifying that routing logic is accurately preserved in the target environment. 

The Migration Tool simplifies this significantly by automatically detecting the pattern from your ICO, generating all necessary artifacts for both the Standard and Pipeline approaches, and providing a structured review step before anything is finalized. 

For the Pipeline Approach in particular, the receiverDetermination XSLT in the Partner Directory becomes the single source of truth for routing logic at runtime making it transparent, manageable, and easy to extend as your integration landscape grows. 

Whether you choose the Standard or Pipeline Approach depends on your landscape and operational requirements but with the Migration Tool, both paths are fully supported and ready for use.
